q: In a civil collision trial, plaintiff's counsel asks her own eyewitness, “The light was red when the truck entered, wasn't it?” Defense counsel objects. Later, plaintiff offers a photograph of the truck driver's bumper stickers, and defense counsel says only, “Objection, relevance.” Plaintiff's counsel argues that the relevance objection is defective because it doesn't say whether the photo lacks probativeness or materiality. How should the court treat the two objections?
o: The first objection goes to the form of the question; the relevance objection is sufficient without naming a prong.
Both objections go to admissibility, so each must cite the specific rule and the specific prong the evidence fails.
The relevance objection must be overruled as stated, because it doesn't identify whether materiality or probativeness is missing.
Neither is proper, because the FRE govern only admissibility and leave the form of questions to trial-advocacy custom.
oe: Correct. Objections can attack the form of a question (leading, compound) or the admissibility of the evidence. Under the FRE a relevance objection doesn't have to distinguish probativeness from materiality (Class 2 trial note).
Leading is a form objection; it concerns how the question is asked, not whether the evidence is admissible. And no prong-specific statement is required for relevance.
The FRE don't require the objector to choose between the 401(a) and 401(b) prongs.

Rule 611(c) itself addresses leading questions, and form objections are routine. The Class 1 slides distinguish form objections (trial advocacy) from admissibility objections (this course), but both are proper.

q: A litigant argues that a 2004 appellate decision construing Rule 407 is no longer good law because Rule 407 was rewritten in 2011, and that the court should apply only the dictionary meaning of the current text. The opposing party responds by citing the House Judiciary Committee report on the rule. Which statement best describes how the court should proceed?
o: The restyling didn't change substance, so the case still guides; read the text with its history and notes, under Rule 102.
The Supreme Court promulgated the rules, so its intent controls and congressional committee reports carry no weight.
The 2011 restyling rewrote substance, so pre-2011 decisions apply only where the court finds the wording unchanged.
Legislative history matters only for privileges, which Congress codified in detail when it enacted the rules in 1975.
oe: Correct. The restyling (effective Dec. 1, 2011) was meant to change style only. Cleary: the text is primary, but legislative history may occasionally override even an apparently plain meaning. Rule 102 states the purposes that guide construction.
The Supreme Court was “merely a conduit” (Douglas, J.; Abel). Congress enacted the rules in 1975 and amended many, so its history matters.
The restyling was expressly not meant to change substance.
Congress scrapped thirteen proposed privilege rules and enacted FRE 501, which leaves privilege largely to the courts. It did not codify detailed privileges.
topic: Foundations & jury secrecy — Interpreting the FRE · 102 · 501

q: A judge excludes a spouse's testimony about a highly probative private conversation with the defendant, citing a privilege. A juror who later learns of the ruling complains that “the rules are supposed to help us find the truth.” Which explanation best fits the ruling?
o: Some evidence rules serve public policies other than accurate fact-finding, such as protecting relationships through privileges.
The ruling must rest on unreliability, since evidence rules exclude only evidence that jurors cannot properly evaluate.
The ruling reflects Rule 403, because highly probative evidence of private conversations is always unfairly prejudicial.
The ruling is error, because Rule 402 makes all relevant evidence admissible and a privilege isn't a rule of evidence.
oe: Correct. The slides list several reasons for evidence rules: saving time, constitutional protections, truthful outcomes, public policies like privileges, and relevance and reliability. Privileges deliberately sacrifice probative evidence for policy.
Privileges exclude reliable evidence. Reliability is only one of several rationales.
403 targets unfair prejudice, not privileged communications, and favors admission of probative evidence.
402 admits relevant evidence unless the Constitution, a statute, the rules, or other Supreme Court rules provide otherwise. Privileges are such an exception.
topic: Foundations & jury secrecy — Why evidence rules exist

q: After a federal jury convicts a defendant of an assault in a parking garage, a juror's affidavit reports: (1) during trial, another juror went to the garage at night, measured the lighting with his phone, and told the jury it was “bright as day,” undercutting the defense's mistaken-identity theory; (2) the jurors were exhausted from playing cards late at the hotel; and (3) the garage report “is what changed three votes.” What may the court consider on the motion for a new trial?
o: Testimony that the juror visited the garage and reported his measurements, but nothing about how it affected the votes.
All three matters, because each describes conduct and circumstances rather than any juror's actual reasoning about guilt.
Only the exhaustion, because fatigue is an objective physical condition rather than part of the jury's deliberations.
Nothing at all, because each of the three matters reached the other jurors only while they were deliberating in private.
oe: Correct. A juror's independent investigation brings extraneous prejudicial information into deliberations (606(b)(2)(A)). But even within an exception, jurors can't testify about the effect on their votes or mental processes; the court judges prejudice objectively.
Exhaustion from card games is internal (like intoxication in Tanner), and the vote-change statement is barred testimony about the effect on votes.
Tanner treats juror incompetence from intoxication, fatigue and similar conditions as internal.
Too broad. The extraneous-information exception covers exactly this kind of outside fact-gathering.
topic: Foundations & jury secrecy — 606(b)(2)(A) · effect on votes

q: During a federal drug trial, the defendant's cousin approached a juror at a gas station and said, “People who convict my family regret it.” The juror didn't report it. After the guilty verdict, she signs an affidavit describing the encounter and adding that she “voted guilty to prove I wasn't scared,” and that the foreperson had bullied the holdouts. Which parts may the court receive?
o: Her description of the cousin's statement only.
Her description of the encounter plus her explanation of her vote, since the exception opens the whole subject.
Her description of the encounter and the foreperson's bullying, since both are pressure applied to jurors.
None of it, because the threat came from the defendant's own relative and he cannot benefit from it.
oe: Correct. A threat from someone outside the jury is an outside influence (606(b)(2)(B)). Her account of why she voted is barred (effect on her vote), and the foreperson's pressure is internal to deliberations.
An exception lets the juror testify that the influence occurred. It never opens her mental processes.
Pressure among jurors is the core of what 606(b)(1) protects.
The rule's text concerns what the juror may testify about. Whether the defendant can obtain relief given his family's misconduct is a separate remedial question, not a 606(b) bar.

q: In a federal negligence trial, all twelve jurors agreed on damages of $250,000, but the foreperson wrote “$25,000” on the verdict form, which was read and recorded. The next day a juror tells the clerk about the error. May the juror testify to correct it?
o: Yes; a juror may testify that a mistake was made in entering the verdict on the verdict form.
No; any juror testimony about what the jury agreed on necessarily reveals its deliberations and is barred.
Only if the error resulted from an outside influence improperly brought to bear on the foreperson.
Yes, and the juror may also explain that several jurors privately thought $25,000 was too low an award.
oe: Correct. 606(b)(2)(C) (covered in Class 1) permits testimony about clerical errors in recording the verdict actually reached.
The verdict-form exception exists precisely for this situation.
The verdict-form exception is independent of the outside-influence exception.
Testimony is limited to the clerical mistake; jurors' views of the amount are mental processes.

q: Variation: The form correctly says “$25,000,” as the jury voted, but a juror reports that the jurors believed the judge would automatically multiply the award by ten. May the juror testify?
o: No; misunderstanding the instructions is a mental process, not a mistake in entering the verdict on the form.
Yes, under 606(b)(2)(C), because the recorded verdict doesn't reflect what the jurors actually intended to award.
Yes, because a misunderstanding of the court's instructions counts as extraneous prejudicial information.
Yes, because the Sixth Amendment overrides 606(b) whenever a verdict rests on a legal misunderstanding.
oe: Correct. 606(b)(2)(C) covers transcription errors. An error in how jurors understood the law goes to their reasoning, which 606(b)(1) bars.
The form records exactly what they voted. Their mistaken assumption about the instructions is internal.
The court's own instructions aren't outside information; how jurors construed them is internal.
Peña-Rodriguez's constitutional exception is limited to clear racial animus.
topic: Foundations & jury secrecy — Clerical error vs. misunderstanding

q: After a federal fraud conviction, the defendant learns that several jurors used cocaine at lunch during trial. He moves for an evidentiary hearing with juror testimony, arguing that the Sixth Amendment guarantees a competent jury. A courtroom deputy is also prepared to testify that she saw a juror asleep. Which ruling is most consistent with Tanner v. United States?
o: Refuse the juror testimony but consider the deputy; voir dire, observation, juror reports and nonjuror evidence protect competence.
Hear the jurors, because drugs are substances brought in from outside the jury room and so qualify as an outside influence.
Hear the jurors, because Congress enacted the House version of 606(b), which allows testimony about objective juror misconduct.
Disregard the deputy too, because 606(b) bars all evidence of juror misconduct from any source once a verdict is returned.
oe: Correct. Tanner held intoxication is internal, not an outside influence, and relied on those other safeguards. Nonjuror evidence remains available.
The majority said drugs and alcohol are no more an outside influence than a virus, poorly prepared food, or lack of sleep.
The Senate version, which barred testimony about anything occurring during deliberations, became law.
606(b) limits juror testimony and affidavits. Tanner itself contemplated nonjuror evidence such as courtroom personnel.
topic: Foundations & jury secrecy — Tanner · safeguards · history

q: Variation: The defendant's appellate brief adopts the Tanner dissent. Which argument would it make?
o: 606(b) doesn't reach matters unrelated to deliberations, and courts can tell minor indispositions from intoxicants.
The common law always allowed juror testimony about misconduct, so 606(b) should be read narrowly to preserve that.
Drug use is extraneous prejudicial information, because cocaine is a fact the jurors brought into the jury room.
Voir dire is the only adequate protection, so the court must re-examine every juror under oath about drug use.
oe: Correct. The dissent read 606(b)'s text as limited to deliberations, mental processes and effects on votes, and rejected the majority's slippery slope as a matter of line drawing.
The common law flatly barred juror impeachment of verdicts except for extraneous influence.
Cocaine isn't information about the case; the dissent's argument was about the scope of 606(b)(1), not 606(b)(2)(A).
The dissent didn't argue for renewed voir dire; it argued 606(b) didn't bar testimony about intoxication at all.
pre: After a federal fraud conviction, the defendant learns that several jurors used cocaine at lunch during trial. He moves for an evidentiary hearing with juror testimony, arguing that the Sixth Amendment guarantees a competent jury. A courtroom deputy is also prepared to testify that she saw a juror asleep. Which ruling is most consistent with Tanner v. United States?

q: In a federal wrongful-death trial from a truck crash, a juror answered “no” when asked whether anyone close to her had been in a serious accident. After a defense verdict, another juror's affidavit says that during deliberations the juror revealed her son had caused a fatal crash and said a lawsuit “would have ruined his life.” The plaintiff moves for a new trial. Which is correct?
o: The affidavit is barred, but she may prove the dishonesty otherwise: a false answer to a material question that would have supported removal.
The affidavit is admissible under 606(b)(2)(A), because the son's fatal crash is a fact from outside the trial record and was never tested by either party.
The affidavit is admissible, because 606(b) applies only to criminal verdicts and this is a civil wrongful-death case.
A new trial is automatic once any juror is shown to have given an inaccurate answer to a voir dire question.
oe: Correct. Warger applied 606(b) even to proof of voir dire dishonesty and held a juror's past experiences aren't “extraneous prejudicial information.” The slides give the two-step test for a new trial.
Warger rejected exactly this: a juror's own experiences are internal, not extraneous information.
606(b) applies in civil and criminal cases; Warger was civil.
The plaintiff must show dishonesty about a material question and that the truthful answer would have provided a valid basis for removal.

q: After a defendant of Mexican descent is convicted of assault in state court, two jurors sign affidavits. One says a juror remarked that the defendant “mumbled like a lot of immigrants do.” The other says a juror argued, “He did it because he's Mexican, and Mexican men take whatever they want,” and urged others to convict on that basis. Under Peña-Rodriguez, what may the court consider?
o: Only the second statement, which clearly shows the juror relied on ethnic stereotypes to convict.
Both statements, because any ethnic reference made during deliberations triggers the constitutional exception.
Neither, because all the jurors affirmed during voir dire that they could decide the case impartially.
Neither, because ethnic bias is internal and the state's version of 606(b) has no exception covering it.
oe: Correct. The threshold is a clear statement showing racial animus was a significant motivating factor in the vote. Offhand remarks don't qualify.
Offhand comments are not enough; the statement must show reliance on racial stereotypes or animus to convict.
Voir dire answers didn't prevent the Court from requiring the rule to yield in Peña-Rodriguez.
The Sixth Amendment overrides the state rule when the threshold is met.

q: Variation: The trial judge, persuaded by the Peña-Rodriguez dissents and by the state's narrow definition of extraneous information, refuses to consider either affidavit. Which reasoning reflects those sources?
o: Colorado's narrow definition of extraneous information, Thomas's history, and Alito's view that bias type doesn't matter.
Racial bias is “especially pernicious in the administration of justice,” so it must be treated like any other juror bias.
The jury is a defendant's protection against race prejudice, so courts should defer to its verdict without inquiry.
Racial bias is an outside influence because it comes from society at large rather than from the evidence at trial.
oe: Correct. That was Colorado's definition, Justice Thomas's historical point, and Justice Alito's argument that the Sixth Amendment's protection doesn't depend on the nature of the jury's partiality.
That language comes from the majority, which used it to justify the exception.
The majority invoked this idea to require the rule to yield, not to bar inquiry.
No opinion adopted this theory; the majority grounded the exception in the Sixth Amendment, not 606(b)(2)(B).
topic: Foundations & jury secrecy — Colorado rule · the dissents
pre: After a defendant of Mexican descent is convicted of assault in state court, two jurors sign affidavits. One says a juror remarked that the defendant “mumbled like a lot of immigrants do.” The other says a juror argued, “He did it because he's Mexican, and Mexican men take whatever they want,” and urged others to convict on that basis. Under Peña-Rodriguez, what may the court consider?

q: In a federal employment-discrimination suit, a juror's affidavit states that another juror said the Black plaintiff “probably wasn't fired for nothing—you know how they are,” and that the remark swayed the jury. The plaintiff seeks a new trial under Peña-Rodriguez. What is the best assessment?
o: Uncertain; Peña-Rodriguez rests on the Sixth Amendment in criminal cases, and extending it to civil cases is debated.
Clearly admissible, because Peña-Rodriguez created a general exception to 606(b) for racial bias in every case.
Clearly admissible under 606(b)(2)(A), because racial stereotypes are extraneous information about the plaintiff.
Clearly barred, because the Seventh Amendment forbids any judicial inquiry into the basis of a civil jury's verdict.
oe: Correct. The holding addressed racial bias used to convict a criminal defendant; extending it to civil litigants is an open question (Problem I.1).
The Court's reasoning was tied to the Sixth Amendment in criminal cases.
Stereotypes jurors bring with them are internal, like past experiences in Warger.
Nothing settles that question; the issue is open.
topic: Foundations & jury secrecy — Problem I.1 · civil cases

q: A defendant is charged with burglary, which requires intent to steal. The prosecution offers four items found on his phone. Which item is irrelevant to intent?
o: A list of his overdue library books.
A chatbot history that begins “how to disable a home alarm.”
A text that afternoon: “They're away tonight, I'm getting the jewelry.”
A browser search the day before for “resale value of gold chains.”
oe: Correct. It has no tendency to make intent to steal more or less probable, so it's irrelevant and inadmissible under 402.
Planning to defeat an alarm makes intent to enter and steal more probable.
Highly probative of intent to steal.
Some tendency to show a plan to steal and sell jewelry; under 401 that's enough. “A brick is not a wall.”

q: State law defines murder as killing “purposely or knowingly” and a separate statute provides that voluntary intoxication “may not be taken into consideration” in determining the mental state. The defendant offers a toxicologist's testimony that he was heavily intoxicated. How should the court rule?
o: Exclude it as immaterial; the statute makes intoxication not “of consequence” to the mental element.
Admit it, because intoxication always tends to make purposeful or knowing conduct less probable.
Admit it, because excluding defense evidence about the defendant's mental state violates due process.
Exclude it under 403 as confusing, while recognizing that intoxication remains a material fact.
oe: Correct. Materiality comes from the substantive law. Montana v. Egelhoff upheld a statute like this, which effectively redefined the mental element.
It may be probative, but it isn't material once the law makes intoxication irrelevant to the elements.
Egelhoff rejected that argument.
The cleaner ground is materiality: the fact isn't of consequence at all.

q: In a bank-robbery prosecution, the defendant concedes in his opening statement that he was in the bank but says he was a customer. The prosecution then offers a teller's testimony identifying him as present. The defense objects that the testimony is irrelevant because presence is undisputed. What is the best ruling?
o: Overrule; a fact needn't be disputed to be of consequence, and any duplication concern belongs under 403.
Sustain; once the defendant concedes his presence, that fact is no longer of consequence to the action.
Sustain; evidence offered on a point the defense has conceded is cumulative as a matter of law.
Overrule, but only if the prosecution first shows the defendant's concession about his presence was false.
oe: Correct. The 1972 Advisory Committee's Note to 401 says the fact to which evidence is directed need not be in dispute. Old Chief handled the concession question under 403, not 401.
Concession doesn't render evidence irrelevant.
Cumulativeness is a discretionary 403 judgment, not automatic.
No such requirement exists.

q: A woman charged with aiding a killing claims self-defense. She testifies that her boyfriend, the deceased, bragged to her that he once stabbed a man in the neck with a pen. She offers a court record of his conviction for that stabbing, which she never saw. The trial judge excludes it as irrelevant to her state of mind. How did the en banc Ninth Circuit view similar evidence?
o: As relevant, because it corroborates her testimony that he told her about the stabbing.
As irrelevant, because only facts she actually knew could have affected her state of mind.
As admissible character evidence of the victim's violence under Rule 405(b)'s specific-acts provision.
As relevant only to whether he actually stabbed someone, which is the material issue in self-defense.
oe: Correct. The trial court asked whether the records bore on her state of mind; the appeals court asked whether they bore on her testimony about her state of mind.
That was the trial court's framing, which the en banc court rejected.
405(b) requires character to be an essential element, and self-defense doesn't make it one (Classes 8–9). The James court's theory was corroboration.
Whether he actually stabbed someone isn't itself material; what matters is her reasonable belief.

q: Variation: Her daughter, who fired the shot, testified that the deceased had his hands up and that she didn't fear him. During deliberations the jury asks to see the conviction record. What is the strongest argument for keeping it out?
o: Under 403, proof he really stabbed a man risks jurors deciding he deserved to be shot.
The daughter's testimony makes the record irrelevant, because it shows no one actually feared him.
A jury's question during deliberations can never be answered by sending back a new exhibit.
The record is barred by 404(a)(1), because it is character evidence about a person who isn't a party.
oe: Correct. That was the dissent's 403 concern. The daughter's testimony doesn't change relevance, which turns on the mother's state of mind.
The issue is the mother's belief when she handed over the gun, which the daughter's testimony doesn't address.
The real question is admissibility, not the procedure for answering the jury.
404(a)(1) applies to any person, but the corroboration theory isn't propensity reasoning.
pre: A woman charged with aiding a killing claims self-defense. She testifies that her boyfriend, the deceased, bragged to her that he once stabbed a man in the neck with a pen. She offers a court record of his conviction for that stabbing, which she never saw. The trial judge excludes it as irrelevant to her state of mind. How did the en banc Ninth Circuit view similar evidence?

q: A man is charged with killing a witness who had accused the defendant's best friend of fraud. To show motive, the prosecution calls a court clerk to testify that at a hearing four days before the killing, the friend's bail was revoked. The defendant wasn't at the hearing, but the friend's sister, who attended, lives with the defendant. The defense objects that the testimony is irrelevant without proof the defendant knew. What should the court do?
o: Admit it if a reasonable jury could find he learned of the hearing, or admit it subject to later connection.
Exclude it unless the judge first finds by a preponderance of the evidence that he actually knew of the hearing.
Admit it unconditionally, because motive evidence never depends on what the defendant himself knew.
Exclude it, because the clerk's account of a hearing in another case is inadmissible hearsay.
oe: Correct. This is conditional relevance under 104(b). As in Cox, an inference of knowledge from regular contact with someone who attended suffices; the judge doesn't weigh credibility or find the fact.
That's the 104(a) standard. Huddleston applies 104(b)'s lenient sufficiency test to conditional relevance.
A motive based on retaliation for the hearing exists only if he knew about it.
The question tests conditional relevance; the clerk testifies to what happened, offered to show its effect on the defendant.

q: Two preliminary questions arise in a fraud trial: (1) whether an email from the defendant to his lawyer is protected by attorney-client privilege, and (2) whether the defendant ever received a warning letter the government offers to show his knowledge. Who decides each, and by what standard?
o: The judge decides privilege under 104(a); for the letter, the judge asks only if a jury could find receipt.
The jury decides both questions, because each one turns on a disputed question of historical fact.
The judge decides both questions by a preponderance of the evidence under Rule 104(a).
The judge decides both questions beyond a reasonable doubt, because this is a criminal prosecution.
oe: Correct. Admissibility questions like privilege are for the judge (Bourjaily: preponderance). Conditional facts are for the jury once there's sufficient evidence (Huddleston).
Privilege is a preliminary question of admissibility for the judge.
Receipt of the letter is a conditional-relevance fact under 104(b).
Neither preliminary standard is beyond a reasonable doubt.

q: In a murder case, the prosecution proves the defendant bought a hunting rifle of the type used in the killing the day before it occurred. The defense shows it was the opening day of deer season and that the store sold over 300 of that model that week. What is the best evaluation?
o: Still relevant; the defense has exposed weak links, which go to weight and to any 403 balance.
Irrelevant once common sales are shown, because the purchase no longer singles out the defendant.
Inadmissible under 104(b) until the prosecution proves that no other buyer committed the crime.
Inadmissible character evidence, because buying a rifle suggests a violent disposition.
oe: Correct. As the slides put it, relevance always depends on the other information we have, and sharp lawyers identify the missing links. The evidence still has some tendency, so it clears 401.
Evidence needn't single anyone out; “a brick is not a wall.”
104(b) addresses facts on which relevance depends, not elimination of alternatives.
Buying a rifle used in the crime is offered for opportunity and means, not character.

q: Two days after a store robbery, officers approach the defendant on the street to ask questions and he runs. At trial the prosecution offers the flight as evidence of guilt. The defendant had an outstanding warrant for an unrelated probation violation at the time. Which link in the prosecution's chain is weakest?
o: From consciousness of guilt to guilt about the robbery, since he may have fled because of the warrant.
From his behavior to flight, because running from officers on a public street is always ambiguous conduct.
From consciousness of guilt about the robbery to actual guilt, because innocent people never fear accusation.
No link is weak, because the law presumes that flight from police shows consciousness of guilt.
oe: Correct. The four links are: behavior → flight; flight → consciousness of guilt; → consciousness of guilt about this crime; → actual guilt. The warrant breaks the third link.
He clearly ran from officers. The weaker link is why.
Possible, but the warrant specifically undermines the third link.
There is no presumption; flight evidence is circumstantial and often weak.

q: Variation: The defendant wants to explain to the jury that he ran because of the warrant, but doing so will reveal his prior conviction. He argues that admitting the flight evidence is unfairly prejudicial. What is the prosecution's best response?
o: The prior offense is old and dissimilar, so the prejudice doesn't substantially outweigh the flight evidence.
The defendant has no right to explain his flight to the jury once the prosecution has proved it occurred.
Prior convictions are always admissible to rebut a defendant's innocent explanation of his flight.
Flight evidence is exempt from Rule 403 because it is circumstantial evidence of consciousness of guilt.
oe: Correct. Problems 1.9 and 1.10 make this point: explaining flight can expose other bad acts, so the prejudice argument is real. But an old, dissimilar, or trivial prior reduces the danger.
He may offer an innocent explanation; the question is 403 balancing.
No such rule exists.
403 applies to all relevant evidence.
pre: Two days after a store robbery, officers approach the defendant on the street to ask questions and he runs. At trial the prosecution offers the flight as evidence of guilt. The defendant had an outstanding warrant for an unrelated probation violation at the time. Which link in the prosecution's chain is weakest?

q: In a Massachusetts prosecution, a young Black man fled when officers approached him in a neighborhood where police frequently stop and frisk Black men. The prosecution offers the flight as consciousness of guilt. The defense wants to call a community member to testify that running from police is common in the neighborhood among people with nothing to hide. What is the best ruling under Warren and the critical-race critique?
o: Admit the testimony if the witness is qualified, because it makes the flight less probative of guilt.
Exclude it as irrelevant, because general community practice says nothing about this particular defendant.
Exclude the flight evidence automatically whenever the defendant belongs to a heavily policed group.
Admit the testimony, but only as character evidence of the defendant's peaceful and law-abiding nature.
oe: Correct. Warren recognized that repeated racial profiling suggests reasons for flight unrelated to guilt, and the slides note a qualified lay community witness may testify to this.
It bears directly on how much weight the flight deserves.
Warren reduces the inference; it doesn't create a per se rule of exclusion.
It isn't character evidence; it explains an alternative reason for flight.

q: A defendant charged with arson tells investigators he was home alone all night. Cell-site records later show he was across town near the fire. He objects to the prosecution's use of his false statement, arguing that lying about his whereabouts doesn't prove he set the fire. Which response is best?
o: A false exculpatory statement shows consciousness of guilt; it needn't prove the arson by itself.
The statement is inadmissible hearsay, because it was made out of court to investigators.
The statement is inadmissible, because a lie to police shows only a dishonest character trait.
The statement is relevant only if the prosecution first proves he lied because he set the fire.
oe: Correct. Lies to investigators tend to show guilty knowledge (Brother's Keeper clip), and relevance needs only some tendency.
His own statement offered against him isn't barred on that ground, and the question concerns relevance.
It's offered for consciousness of guilt about this crime, not general dishonesty.
Alternative reasons go to weight; the inference needn't be certain.

q: In an embezzlement trial, the prosecution offers a recording in which the defendant tells a friend, “I took the money and I'd do it again.” The defense objects under 403 that the recording is “devastating” and will make it nearly impossible to win. How should the court rule?
o: Overrule; damaging evidence isn't unfairly prejudicial, and the danger must substantially outweigh its value.
Sustain; evidence so powerful that it would effectively decide the case is unfairly prejudicial under 403.
Sustain; Rule 403 favors exclusion of recorded confessions because juries overvalue them.
Overrule; Rule 403 never applies to a party's own statements offered against that party.
oe: Correct. Probative evidence always hurts the other side. Unfair prejudice means a tendency to suggest decision on an improper, often emotional, basis.
That conflates probative force with unfair prejudice.
403 favors admission.
403 applies to all relevant evidence.

q: A defendant is charged with possessing a firearm after a felony conviction. His prior felony was armed robbery with a handgun. He offers to stipulate that he has a qualifying conviction, but the prosecutor insists on introducing the judgment naming the crime. How should the court rule?
o: Accept the stipulation and exclude the crime's name, since only felon status is at issue.
Admit the judgment, because a prosecutor is always entitled to prove its case with evidence of its choice.
Exclude the judgment as irrelevant, because the defendant has conceded the only element it proves.
Admit the judgment with a limiting instruction, because an instruction cures any risk of prejudice.
oe: Correct. Old Chief held it an abuse of discretion to reject the stipulation. The record remains relevant (a concession doesn't make it irrelevant), but the available alternative discounts its value under 403.
That's the general rule, but Old Chief made an exception for pure status elements.
Concession doesn't make evidence irrelevant; the analysis is under 403.
That was the dissent's approach; the majority required accepting the admission.

q: Variation: In a murder trial, the defendant offers to stipulate that he caused the victim's death and asks the court to exclude the 911 call and crime-scene video. What is the best ruling?
o: Old Chief is limited to status; narrative evidence isn't replaced by a stipulation, though 403 can trim items.
The stipulation must be accepted, because Old Chief requires courts to accept any concession the defense offers.
The video must be excluded as cumulative, because the stipulation already establishes the fact it shows.
The court must give a limiting instruction in place of accepting or rejecting the defendant's stipulation.
oe: Correct. Justice Souter's three reasons explain why the general rule favors the prosecution's choice.
Old Chief's holding is confined to proof of felon status.
Narrative evidence isn't cumulative merely because a bare fact is conceded.
Limiting instructions don't resolve whether the prosecution must accept a stipulation.
pre: A defendant is charged with possessing a firearm after a felony conviction. His prior felony was armed robbery with a handgun. He offers to stipulate that he has a qualifying conviction, but the prosecutor insists on introducing the judgment naming the crime. How should the court rule?

q: In a robbery case, the eyewitnesses saw a getaway car described as a red convertible driven by a man with a tattoo and a woman with dyed purple hair. A statistics professor, with no data, assigns probabilities to each trait (red convertible 1/20, tattoo 1/5, purple hair 1/50, and so on), multiplies them, and testifies there is a one-in-ten-million chance an innocent couple would match. The defense objects. What is the best ruling under People v. Collins?
o: Exclude it: the probabilities are invented and dependent, and it distracts jurors from the real question.
Admit it, because the product rule is mathematically valid and the jury can weigh any flaws in the inputs.
Exclude it, because mathematical evidence is never admissible to prove a defendant's identity.
Admit it with a limiting instruction telling the jurors that the professor's numbers are only estimates.
oe: Correct. Collins found both prejudicial errors: no adequate foundation in evidence or statistical theory, and distraction from weighing the actual evidence.
The rule is valid only for independent events with real data, which were missing.
Collins doesn't ban math; DNA statistics are routinely admitted.
An instruction can't cure testimony with no foundation.

q: Variation: (1) In a burglary case, a DNA analyst testifies that the crime-scene profile matches the defendant and would occur in about 1 in 48 billion people, based on validated population databases. (2) In a civil case, a plaintiff hit by a bus offers only proof that Blue Bus Co. runs 80% of the town's buses. Which statement is most accurate?
o: The DNA figure is admissible and should be explained; the bus statistic is relevant but meets intuitive resistance.
Both are inadmissible under Collins, because each relies on multiplying probabilities under the product rule.
Both are conclusive, because each one, standing alone, exceeds the applicable burden of proof.
Only the bus statistic is admissible, because civil cases allow probability evidence and criminal cases don't.
oe: Correct. Collins condemned bad math, not math. DNA uses the same product rule with real data. The Blue Bus problem shows that people resist purely statistical proof, preferring even a weak eyewitness.
Collins doesn't bar statistics with an adequate foundation.
Admissibility and sufficiency are separate; neither is conclusive.
DNA probability evidence is routinely admitted in criminal cases. Market-share liability in asbestos cases is another accepted use.
topic: Rule 403 and 105 — Sound probability evidence · Blue Bus
pre: In a robbery case, the eyewitnesses saw a getaway car described as a red convertible driven by a man with a tattoo and a woman with dyed purple hair. A statistics professor, with no data, assigns probabilities to each trait (red convertible 1/20, tattoo 1/5, purple hair 1/50, and so on), multiplies them, and testifies there is a one-in-ten-million chance an innocent couple would match. The defense objects. What is the best ruling under People v. Collins?

q: At a murder trial the defense concedes the victim's death, its cause, and the extent of her wounds, but disputes identity. The prosecution offers four photos of the body showing the angle and depth of the wounds, which a juror specifically asked about, and two autopsy photos that no witness discusses. The court admits all six, and the defendant is convicted on strong evidence. On appeal, what result is most likely under Bocharski?
o: No abuse of discretion on the wound photos; error on the autopsy photos, but harmless.
Reversal, because gruesome photos of facts the defense concedes are always unfairly prejudicial.
Affirmance on all six, because photos of a homicide victim are always relevant to the cause of death.
Reversal, because a juror's question can never justify admitting evidence the defense has conceded.
oe: Correct. That was Bocharski's exhibit-by-exhibit result, reviewed for abuse of discretion.
Photos can still have probative value on contested details; the analysis is case-specific.
Relevant, yes, but the autopsy photos' slight probative value was outweighed.
The juror's question helped show the wound photos had probative value.

q: Variation: Defense counsel cites a study for the claim that gruesome photographs dramatically increase conviction rates. What did the Grady et al. meta-analysis actually find?
o: Gruesome vs. neutral photos had a small effect; photos vs. none had a larger effect.
Gruesome photographs roughly doubled conviction rates in every study the researchers examined.
Photographs of any kind had no measurable effect on the decisions jurors reached.
Judges proved more affected by gruesome photographs than the jurors who saw them.
oe: Correct. The meta-analysis found g = 0.077 (gruesome vs. neutral) and g = 0.450 (photos vs. none), and urged caution before blanket claims of prejudice.
No such finding.
The no-photo comparison showed a meaningful effect.
The study addressed juror and mock-juror decisions.

The prosecution offers four photos of the body showing the angle and depth of the wounds, which a juror specifically asked about, and two autopsy photos that no witness discusses. The court admits all six, and the defendant is convicted on strong evidence. On appeal, what result is most likely under Bocharski?

q: In a homicide trial, the prosecution offers a computer-generated animation of the shooting prepared by its experts, and separately wants a detective to walk the jury through a PowerPoint timeline of phone records already in evidence. The defense objects that the animation is “far more persuasive than live testimony.” What is the best approach?
o: Admit the animation if authenticated, relevant and not barred by 403; the timeline is an illustrative aid, not evidence.
Exclude the animation, because computer recreations are inherently speculative and more persuasive than testimony.
Admit both as exhibits and send both to the jury room, because each helps the jurors understand the evidence.
Admit the animation only if the defense can afford to commission an animation of its own to rebut it.
oe: Correct. Serge applies ordinary rules to demonstrative animations. Proposed 611(d) distinguishes illustrative aids, which are used but not admitted.
Serge rejected a special rule for CGAs.
Illustrative aids generally don't go to deliberations.
The slides note cost-disparity arguments, but they aren't a rule of admissibility.

q: In a federal murder trial, the prosecution calls the victim's brother to show a photo of the victim at his child's birthday party and to describe him as “the gentlest person you'd ever meet.” The defense, which doesn't contest the victim's identity or death, objects. What is the best ruling?
o: The photo may be allowed briefly under 403, but describing his gentleness is character evidence of peacefulness.
Both are admissible, because the prosecution may always humanize a homicide victim for the jury.
Both must be excluded, because the victim's life has no bearing on any fact of consequence in the case.
Both are admissible, because Old Chief requires the court to accept the prosecution's chosen narrative in full.
oe: Correct. Minnesota's doctrine (State v. Graham) and the Chauvin ruling allow showing the victim was a loved human being; Judge Cahill drew the line at propensity for peacefulness.
Peacefulness testimony is character evidence with its own rules.
Some probative or contextual value is recognized; the issue is 403 discretion.
Old Chief supports narrative evidence, but it doesn't override 403 or the character rules.

q: In a joint civil fraud trial, a letter written by Defendant A is admissible against A but not against Defendant B. B's counsel doesn't ask for any instruction. After a verdict against both, B argues the court erred by failing to tell the jury not to use the letter against B. Separately, the plaintiff had called a fifth witness to repeat an undisputed fact. Which is correct?
o: 105 requires an instruction only on timely request, and the fifth witness could be limited as cumulative.
The court had to give the instruction on its own, because Rule 105 applies whether or not anyone asks.
The letter was inadmissible against both, because evidence admissible against only one party must be excluded.
Cumulative evidence can never be excluded when it is offered to prove a fact that is undisputed.
oe: Correct. 105 says the court, on timely request, must restrict the evidence and instruct. Cumulative evidence is a 403 danger.
The rule is triggered by a timely request.
105 exists precisely to let such evidence in with a limit.
Needlessly cumulative evidence is a classic 403 ground.

q: A defendant is charged with witness tampering for texting a witness, “Do a Frank Pentangeli,” a reference to a mob movie in which a witness recants after seeing a crime boss in the courtroom. The prosecution wants to play the three-minute movie clip. The defense argues a short description or transcript would suffice. How should the court evaluate the objection?
o: A less prejudicial alternative is a proper 403 factor, but it doesn't require excluding the clip.
The clip must be excluded whenever a less vivid alternative, such as a transcript, is available.
The clip must be admitted, because the defendant himself chose to reference the movie in his text.
The clip is irrelevant, because a scene from a fictional movie cannot prove what a real person intended.
oe: Correct. The Advisory Committee's Note to 403 makes alternatives relevant. The prosecution can argue the clip isn't gory and a transcript would still mention mob violence.
Alternatives are a factor, not a trump.
His choice raises its probative value but doesn't eliminate 403.
The clip explains what the defendant's message meant.
topic: Rule 403 and 105 — Other means of proof

q: A customer trips on a loose floor mat in a restaurant's entryway and breaks her wrist. The next morning the restaurant pays a handyman $60 to tack the mat down. At trial the manager testifies that securing the mat “would have meant ripping up the whole floor, a $30,000 job.” For which purpose may the plaintiff offer the $60 repair?
o: To impeach the manager and rebut his claim that a precaution wasn't feasible.
To prove negligence, because the repair's low cost shows how careless it was not to act sooner.
To prove negligence, because an outside handyman, not the restaurant itself, made the repair.
For no purpose, because Rule 407 bars all evidence of measures taken after an injury.
oe: Correct. 407 bars subsequent measures to prove negligence, but allows them for impeachment or, if disputed, feasibility. The manager's testimony puts both in play (the $55.26 carpet hypo, Class 4).
That's the forbidden use. 407 aims to encourage repairs, not to aid the jury's search for truth.
The restaurant took the measure through its agent; it's still the defendant's subsequent remedial measure.
407 expressly permits other purposes such as impeachment and disputed feasibility.

q: Variation: The manager doesn't discuss cost, but the restaurant's defense is that the entryway belongs to the landlord, who alone controls it. May the plaintiff offer the repair?
o: Yes, to show the restaurant controlled the entryway, since control is disputed, with a limiting instruction.
No, because control of leased premises can be proven only by the lease and not by later conduct.
Yes, and once it is admitted the jury may also use the repair as evidence of the restaurant's negligence.
No, because the restyled rule applies the “if disputed” qualifier only to proof of feasibility.
oe: Correct. Ownership and control are permitted purposes “if disputed,” and the 2011 restyling made clear that qualifier covers all three.
Any relevant evidence may prove control.
Admitted for a limited purpose, it may not be used to prove negligence (105).
The restyled text applies “if disputed” to ownership, control and feasibility.
pre: A customer trips on a loose floor mat in a restaurant's entryway and breaks her wrist. The next morning the restaurant pays a handyman $60 to tack the mat down. At trial the manager testifies that securing the mat “would have meant ripping up the whole floor, a $30,000 job.” For which purpose may the plaintiff offer the $60 repair?

q: A child is burned when a space heater tips over. After the incident, the manufacturer adds an automatic tip-over shutoff and a new warning label. In the strict-liability design-defect suit, the plaintiff offers both changes to prove the heater was defective and needed a warning. How should the court rule?
o: Exclude both; since 1997, 407 bars subsequent measures offered to prove a defect or a need for a warning.
Admit both, because 407 protects only negligent defendants and this is a strict-liability claim.
Admit the shutoff but not the label, because a change to a product's design isn't a “measure” under 407.
Admit both to show feasibility, even though the manufacturer concedes a shutoff device was feasible.
oe: Correct. The 1997 amendment resolved the old split over whether 407 applied in strict-liability cases.
That was a pre-1997 minority view.
Both are remedial measures.
Feasibility is a permitted purpose only if disputed.

q: In March a dog bites a mail carrier. In April the owner installs a fence. In June the gate is left open and the dog bites a child. Both victims sue the owner for negligence and offer the fence installation. How does 407 apply?
o: It bars the evidence in the carrier's suit but not in the child's suit.
It bars the evidence in both suits, because the fence was a remedial measure taken after a dog bite.
It bars the evidence in neither suit, because the fence ultimately failed to prevent the second bite.
It bars the evidence in the child's suit only, because the carrier was bitten before the fence went up.
oe: Correct. 407 covers measures taken after the earlier injury at issue (Problem 2.1, Wolf Attack).
As to the child, it wasn't “subsequent” to that harm.
The measure need only be one that would have made the earlier injury less likely.
Backwards. The carrier's injury is the earlier one.

q: A cyclist hits a pothole and sues the paving contractor that resurfaced the road last year. After the crash, the city, which isn't a party, patches the pothole. The cyclist offers the city's repair to show the road was dangerous. What is the most likely ruling?
o: Not barred by 407 in most courts, but it may be excluded under 403 as saying little about the contractor.
Barred by 407, because the rule's passive-voice text covers measures taken by anyone at all.
Admissible to prove negligence without further analysis, because 407 never applies to non-parties.
Admissible only if the city is joined as a defendant, so that its own conduct is properly at issue.
oe: Correct. Most circuits admit third-party repairs (Millennium Partners), since the repair-encouraging policy isn't implicated; some exclude under 403 (Werner v. Upjohn; Raymond).
The passive-voice text might suggest that, but most courts read it as limited to the defendant's own measures.
403 still applies, and relevance to this defendant is weak.
Joinder isn't required for admissibility.

q: A contractor invoices $40,000. Before any complaint, the owner emails: “The work is great and I owe you every penny, but cash is tight. Will you take $30,000 now?” Months later the owner refuses to pay anything, claiming defects, and at a mediation his lawyer says, “We'll pay $15,000; we know the gutters were fine.” Which statement may the contractor offer at trial?
o: The first email, because the claim was not yet disputed as to validity or amount.
The mediation statement, because an admission of fact isn't itself an offer of compromise.
Both, because neither statement actually resulted in a settlement of the contractor's claim.
Neither, because any discussion of how much will be paid on a debt is a compromise offer.
oe: Correct. 408 protects compromises of a disputed claim. An effort to pay an admittedly due amount for less isn't covered (ACN 408).
408(a)(2) bars conduct or statements made during compromise negotiations, including factual admissions.
Failure to settle doesn't remove 408's protection.
The dispute requirement takes the first email outside 408.

q: During settlement talks in a product suit, the defendant's chief engineer says, “Between us, the brake design was rushed.” At trial he testifies the design was thoroughly tested. Separately, a former co-defendant settled with the plaintiff for $200,000 and then testified for the plaintiff. Which use is permitted?
o: The co-defendant's settlement may show bias, but the engineer can't be impeached with his statement.
Both uses are permitted, because impeachment is not an attempt to prove the claim's validity.
Neither use is permitted, because 408 bars all evidence of compromise for every purpose.
The engineer may be impeached, because he is a witness rather than a party to the negotiations.
oe: Correct. 408(a) bars impeachment by prior inconsistent statement (since 2006), while 408(b) allows proof of a witness's bias or prejudice.
408 expressly bars impeachment by prior inconsistent statement or contradiction.
408(b) allows other purposes such as bias.
The statement was made during the party's compromise negotiations; the bar applies.

q: The SEC investigates a broker. In settlement talks with SEC staff, he says, “I moved client money into my account,” and offers to pay $1 million to resolve the matter. Talks fail and he is criminally prosecuted. The prosecution offers both the statement and the offer. How should the court rule?
o: Admit the statement but exclude the offer; the public-office exception reaches statements, not offers.
Exclude both, because 408 applies in criminal cases to exactly the same extent as in civil cases.
Admit both, because all evidence from negotiations with a government agency is usable in a prosecution.
Exclude both, because negotiations with any government agency are plea negotiations under Rule 410.
oe: Correct. The exception applies when negotiations related to a claim by a public office exercising regulatory, investigative or enforcement authority, and it reaches only (a)(2) statements and conduct.
The (a)(2) exception specifically addresses criminal cases.
The offer of compromise under (a)(1) remains protected.
These were civil talks with a regulator, not plea discussions with a prosecutor.

q: Variation: Instead of the SEC, the broker made the statement while negotiating a settlement with a defrauded client's lawyer. May the prosecution offer it in the criminal case?
o: No; statements in settling a private civil claim are generally inadmissible in a later criminal case.
Yes, because Rule 408 never applies in criminal prosecutions, whoever the negotiations were with.
Yes, because the client is a crime victim, which brings the talks within the public-office exception.
No, because the client's lawyer acted as a government agent when negotiating on the client's behalf.
oe: Correct. The 2006 ACN explains that admitting them would discourage parties from admitting fault even when doing so would settle the private matter.
It does; only the public-office exception differs.
That doesn't trigger the public-office exception.
A private lawyer isn't a public office.
pre: The SEC investigates a broker. In settlement talks with SEC staff, he says, “I moved client money into my account,” and offers to pay $1 million to resolve the matter. Talks fail and he is criminally prosecuted. The prosecution offers both the statement and the offer. How should the court rule?

q: Two passengers are injured in the same crash. The driver settles with Passenger 1 for $90,000. Passenger 2 sues and offers the settlement to show the driver knew he was at fault. What is the most likely ruling?
o: Excluded; courts generally apply 408 to compromises with third parties arising from the same events.
Admitted, because 408's text covers only compromises between the parties to this particular lawsuit.
Admitted, because a settlement with a third party is the driver's own statement and a party admission.
Excluded, but only if Passenger 1 objects to disclosure of the terms of her settlement.
oe: Correct. All nine circuits to address it allow exclusion when it advances the policy favoring settlement (e.g., Bradbury, 10th Cir.).
A literal reading suggests that, but courts haven't adopted it.
408 doesn't turn on hearsay categories.
The rule's protection doesn't depend on the third party's objection.

q: After a guest is hurt in a hotel fire, the hotel's insurer and the guest's lawyer begin settlement talks. During the talks, the hotel hires a fire-safety consultant, whose report concedes code violations, and shares it with the guest's lawyer to support a settlement figure. Talks fail. The guest offers the report at trial. What is the most likely ruling?
o: Excluded as a statement made during compromise negotiations by the hotel's agent.
Admitted, because the report was written by a consultant who isn't a party to the lawsuit.
Admitted, because a factual report can never itself be part of compromise negotiations.
Admitted, because the hotel waived 408's protection by sharing the report with the guest.
oe: Correct. In Problem 2.4 (Goldsmith report), most courts would treat such a report as part of the negotiations; otherwise parties would never hire such agents.
A party's agent's statements in negotiations fall within 408.
Statements of fact made in negotiations are covered.
Sharing it in negotiations is exactly what 408 protects.

q: Variation: The hotel, not the guest, wants to show the jury that it offered $500,000, arguing the offer proves it took the claim seriously and the guest's damages are inflated. May it?
o: No; 408 bars compromise evidence “on behalf of any party” to prove validity or amount.
Yes, because Rule 408 protects only the party on the receiving end of a settlement offer.
Yes, because the offer is being used to prove the amount of damages rather than liability.
Yes, provided a hotel representative testifies about the offer and is subject to cross.
oe: Correct. The offeror can't use its own offer either.
The text applies on behalf of any party.
Amount is expressly covered.
Testimony doesn't change the prohibited purpose.
topic: Specialized relevance (407–411) — 408 “on behalf of any party”

q: Right after a rear-end collision, a driver tells the other motorist, “I'm so sorry—I was reading a text. Let me pay your ER bill.” Two weeks later, at a meeting with both lawyers to discuss settling, he says, “I'm sorry I caused this.” Which statements may the injured motorist offer to prove liability?
o: The texting admission and the scene apology, but not the bill offer or the settlement-meeting statement.
None of them, because each statement was made in an effort to resolve the matter without a lawsuit.
All of them, because none of the statements was made in exchange for a release of the claim.
Only the offer to pay the ER bill, because an offer of payment implies an admission of liability.
oe: Correct. 409 excludes only the offer to pay medical expenses, not accompanying statements. The later apology falls under 408 as a statement during compromise negotiations (unless a state apology law protects the scene apology).
Only the medical-expense offer and the negotiation statement are protected.
408 covers negotiations even without a completed settlement, and 409 doesn't require a release.
409 specifically excludes that offer.

q: Variation: A surgeon tells a patient after a complication, “I'm so sorry for what you're going through. We gave you the wrong dosage.” The state has a “partial” apology law. In the malpractice suit, which part is protected?
o: Only the expression of sympathy; a partial apology law doesn't cover the admission of fault.
Both statements, because the state's apology law protects any apology made after an injury.
Neither statement, because state apology laws apply only to criminal prosecutions.
Both statements, because Rule 409 excludes apologies made along with medical care.
oe: Correct. Thirty-four states and D.C. have partial laws protecting sympathy and condolence; only five have full laws covering admissions of fault.
That describes a full apology law.
They're aimed at civil liability, especially malpractice.
409 covers offers to pay medical expenses, not apologies or admissions.
