Let me pay your ER bill.” Two weeks later, at a meeting with both lawyers to discuss settling, he says, “I'm sorry I caused this.” Which statements may the injured motorist offer to prove liability?

q: After a fatal crash, a driver is charged criminally and also sued for wrongful death. In the civil suit, the plaintiff offers four items against the driver. Which is admissible?
o: His guilty plea to a related charge in a separate case, which he never withdrew.
A guilty plea to vehicular homicide that the court later allowed him to withdraw.
His nolo contendere plea to a misdemeanor charge arising from the same crash.
His admissions to the judge during the Rule 11 colloquy on that nolo plea.
oe: Correct. 410 protects only withdrawn guilty pleas, nolo pleas, and related statements; a standing guilty plea isn't covered.
Barred by 410(a)(1).
Barred by 410(a)(2), in civil and criminal cases.
Barred by 410(a)(3).

q: A defendant charged with drug trafficking made three statements: (1) to the assigned federal prosecutor during plea negotiations that failed; (2) to a DEA agent who said he'd “let the prosecutor know you're cooperating,” though the agent had no authority to negotiate; and (3) to the arresting officer, without any discussion of a deal. Which is excluded by 410 in most courts?
o: Only the statement to the prosecutor.
Statements (1) and (2), because the agent promised to relay the cooperation to the prosecutor.
All three, because each was made in the hope of obtaining leniency from the government.
None of them, because Rule 410 protects only formal plea agreements that are later withdrawn.
oe: Correct. 410(a)(4) covers plea discussions with an attorney for the prosecuting authority. An agent without actual or apparent authority isn't enough (Greene). Some courts protect statements made with a reasonable, actual expectation of negotiating (Robertson), but that's the minority approach.
In Greene the Eighth Circuit admitted similar statements to a DEA agent lacking authority.
The arrest statement involved no plea discussion at all.
410(a)(4) covers discussions that didn't result in a plea.

q: During failed plea talks, a defendant tells the prosecutor he was at the warehouse during the theft. At trial he testifies he was out of state. With no waiver, may the prosecution impeach him with his plea-talk statement?
o: No; plea-discussion statements can't be used even to impeach.
Yes; impeachment use is always permitted when a defendant lies on the stand.
Yes; under 410(b)(2), because his trial testimony amounts to perjury.
Yes; Rule 410 protects only statements made to police officers.
oe: Correct. Unlike other evidence rules, 410's bar holds even for impeachment, because defendants wouldn't negotiate otherwise.
Not under 410.
(b)(2) applies in a later prosecution for perjury or false statement, and only if the earlier statement was under oath, on the record, with counsel present.
It applies to statements to prosecutors.

q: Variation: Before the talks, he signed an agreement that his statements could be used to impeach any contrary trial testimony, and another clause allowing use in the government's case-in-chief. What result?
o: The impeachment waiver is enforceable, and several circuits also enforce case-in-chief waivers.
Both waivers are void, because 410 protects the integrity of the plea-bargaining system itself.
Only the case-in-chief waiver is valid, because impeachment waivers coerce a defendant's testimony.
Neither waiver is valid unless a judge approved it on the record before the discussions began.
oe: Correct. Defendants may knowingly and voluntarily waive even fundamental rights, and nothing suggests 410 is nonwaivable (Washburn; Mitchell).
Mezzanatto rejected that argument.
Mezzanatto itself upheld an impeachment waiver.
No judicial approval requirement exists.
pre: During failed plea talks, a defendant tells the prosecutor he was at the warehouse during the theft. At trial he testifies he was out of state. With no waiver, may the prosecution impeach him with his plea-talk statement?

q: In which situation may a statement made during unsuccessful plea discussions with a prosecutor be admitted?
o: The defense offers one favorable statement, and the prosecution offers another from the same talks in fairness.
The defendant is later prosecuted for perjury based on an unsworn statement made in a meeting without counsel.
The prosecution offers it in its case-in-chief because the defendant's guilt is otherwise clear from the evidence.
The statement is offered in a later civil case rather than a criminal case against the same defendant.
oe: Correct. 410(b)(1) is a completeness exception.
410(b)(2) requires the statement to be under oath, on the record, and with counsel present.
Strength of the case is irrelevant to 410.
410 applies in civil and criminal cases.

q: A corporate executive is charged with fraud. Before trial the government offered him immunity if he testified truthfully about wrongdoing at the company; he refused, saying he knew of none. The government has offered evidence that he moved assets into gold bars after colleagues pleaded guilty. He now offers his rejection of immunity as consciousness of innocence. How should the court rule?
o: Admit it; 410 bars only evidence against the defendant, and fairness lets him answer the guilt evidence.
Exclude it, because Rule 410 bars all evidence of plea or immunity negotiations, whoever offers it.
Exclude it as irrelevant, because people refuse immunity for many reasons, including fear of reprisal.
Admit it only if the government consents to disclosure of its immunity negotiations.
oe: Correct. This tracks Biaggi (2d Cir. 1990). Rejecting a plea to a reduced charge is weaker evidence (Problem 2.8), and courts usually exclude a prosecutor's plea offers to protect plea bargaining.
The text bars evidence “against the defendant.”
Alternative explanations (fear of reprisal) go to weight.
Admissibility isn't left to the government's consent.

q: A pedestrian is hit by a landscaping truck and sues Rojas, claiming he owned the truck and employed its driver. Rojas denies owning the truck. The plaintiff offers a liability policy on the truck naming Rojas as the insured. For what purpose may it be admitted?
o: To prove Rojas owned or controlled the truck, with an instruction against using it on negligence.
To prove Rojas was negligent, because owners who carry insurance tend to be less careful.
For no purpose, because evidence that a party was insured is never admissible at trial.
To show Rojas can afford to pay a large verdict, which bears on the amount of damages.
oe: Correct. 411 bars insurance to prove negligence or wrongful conduct but allows other purposes such as agency, ownership or control.
That's the barred use.
411 lists permitted purposes.
Ability to pay isn't a permitted purpose and invites the prejudice 411 guards against.

q: Variation: An adjuster for the defendant's insurer took the plaintiff's recorded statement in the hospital, which the defense uses to impeach her. The adjuster doesn't testify. The plaintiff wants to show he worked for the defendant's insurer, arguing his role made the interview coercive. What is the likely ruling?
o: Excluded; even if bias is a permitted purpose, the employment barely matters here, so 403 keeps it out.
Admitted, because 411 always allows evidence of insurance when it is offered to show a person's bias.
Admitted, because jurors already assume homeowners carry insurance, so there is no prejudice at all.
Excluded, because Rule 411 bars a plaintiff from offering evidence of a defendant's insurance.
oe: Correct. That was the professor's view of Lacher v. Anderson.
It's allowed for bias, but 403 still applies.
Juror awareness reduces prejudice somewhat but doesn't create probative value.
411 isn't party-specific.
pre: A pedestrian is hit by a landscaping truck and sues Rojas, claiming he owned the truck and employed its driver. Rojas denies owning the truck. The plaintiff offers a liability policy on the truck naming Rojas as the insured. For what purpose may it be admitted?

q: In a car-crash trial, insurance has been properly excluded. The judge wants to minimize jurors' speculation about it. Based on the Arizona Jury Project research, which approach is most promising?
o: Tell jurors not to speculate about matters not in evidence and that their information may be incomplete.
Tell jurors that the defendant is uninsured, so they won't assume an insurer will pay any verdict.
Say nothing, because research shows jurors never think about insurance unless someone mentions it.
Tell jurors to assume the defendant is insured, so they won't hesitate to award full damages.
oe: Correct. Deliberations showed jurors discussed insurance in 85% of trials, mostly whether the plaintiff was insured, and researchers suggested educating jurors rather than blindfolding them.
That would be false and creates its own problems.
The project found insurance came up frequently anyway.
Jurors' main worry was a plaintiff's double recovery; such an instruction invites speculation.
topic: Specialized relevance (407–411) — Blindfolding · Arizona Jury Project

q: A commentator argues that Rules 407–411 should be repealed and judges should instead decide each case under Rule 403. Which argument did the advisory committee make for keeping specific exclusionary rules?
o: Pure discretion would cut predictability, undercutting repairs and settlements, and multiply motions in limine.
Rule 403 doesn't apply to repairs, settlements, pleas or insurance, so specific rules are the only tool available.
Specific rules are needed because judges otherwise lack any authority to exclude relevant evidence.
The specific rules admit more evidence than Rule 403 would, which promotes accurate fact-finding.
oe: Correct. The committee listed: expanded discretion (bias, forum shopping); lost predictability; more complex preparation; more motions in limine; and likely separate criminal and civil rules.
403 applies to all relevant evidence; the specific rules are applications of its balancing.
403 gives that authority.
They exclude evidence as a matter of law.

q: A man insulted the defendant's wife on the street. The defendant went home, returned with a pistol, and shot him during a scuffle. The only issue is premeditation. To show the defendant is “a desperate type of criminal,” the prosecutor displays three other handguns and a tear-gas gun found in his apartment, which played no part in the shooting. What is the best ruling?
o: Exclude them; they show only a dangerous character and action in conformity with it.
Admit them, because owning many weapons is relevant to whether the killing was premeditated.
Admit them with a limiting instruction, because Rule 105 cures any propensity concerns.
Exclude them, but only if the defense first offers evidence of the defendant's good character.
oe: Correct. People v. Zackowitz (Cardozo, J.) reversed on these facts. The two policy concerns are excessive weight and conviction for bad character.
The only path to premeditation runs through character: he's the kind of man who kills deliberately.
A limiting instruction can't save evidence whose only use is forbidden.
The ban applies regardless; the prosecution can't open character itself.

q: Variation: Store records show the defendant bought the three handguns an hour after his wife told him of the insult. Must the court admit them?
o: No, but it may; buying guns after the insult shows preparation, but 404(b)(2) never requires admission.
Yes, because preparation is a listed exception to the character ban, and listed exceptions are mandatory.
No, because evidence of weapons the defendant didn't use is always propensity evidence.
Yes, because Rule 403 doesn't apply to evidence offered for a purpose listed in 404(b)(2).
oe: Correct. The slides make both points: the purchase timing changes the inference to preparation, and 404(b)(2) permits rather than requires admission. The Zackowitz dissent similarly argued the weapons showed he could carry out his threat.
The 404(b)(2) purposes aren't exceptions, and admission is discretionary.
Timing can give it a non-character purpose.
403 always applies.
pre: A man insulted the defendant's wife on the street. The defendant went home, returned with a pistol, and shot him during a scuffle. The only issue is premeditation. To show the defendant is “a desperate type of criminal,” the prosecutor displays three other handguns and a tear-gas gun found in his apartment, which played no part in the shooting. What is the best ruling?

q: In a civil negligence suit after an intersection crash, the defendant driver calls (1) a neighbor who will testify the driver has a reputation as an extremely careful driver, and (2) a coworker who has ridden with the driver to work daily for five years and will testify that the driver comes to a full stop and looks both ways at that exact intersection every time. Which is admissible?
o: Only the coworker's testimony, as evidence of habit under Rule 406.
Only the neighbor's testimony, because reputation is the proper form of character proof under 405(a).
Both, because a civil defendant facing a stigmatizing claim may offer evidence of good character.
Neither, because habit evidence requires corroboration by an eyewitness to the crash itself.
oe: Correct. 404(a)(2)'s exceptions apply only in criminal cases (the 2006 amendment ended the Perrin v. Anderson approach), so carefulness is barred character. A specific, regular response to a recurring situation is habit.
405(a) governs form only when character is otherwise admissible; here it isn't.
That was the Perrin rationale, rejected by the 2006 amendment.
406 allows habit regardless of corroboration or an eyewitness.

q: A defendant charged with wire fraud calls a neighbor who testifies to the defendant's excellent reputation for honesty. On direct, defense counsel also asks the neighbor to describe the time the defendant returned a lost wallet with $500 in it. On cross, the prosecutor, who has a police report, asks, “Have you heard that in 2016 he was arrested for check-kiting?” Which rulings are correct?
o: Exclude the wallet story; allow the arrest question, with an instruction that it only tests the witness.
Allow both, because specific acts are the most convincing proof of character and the door is open.
Bar both, because an arrest isn't a conviction and the wallet story isn't reputation evidence.
Allow the wallet story but bar the question, because the prosecution can't attack unoffered character.
oe: Correct. 405(a) limits direct to reputation or opinion; specific instances are allowed on cross to test the witness. Michelson upheld “Have you heard?” questions with a good-faith basis.
The ACN says specific acts are most convincing but most prone to prejudice, surprise and delay, so 405(a) bars them on direct.
Michelson allowed the arrest question because it tests the witness's knowledge of the reputation.
The defendant did put his honesty in issue, opening the door to rebuttal and cross.

q: Variation: The neighbor moved away eight years ago and admits on voir dire that he has talked about the defendant with only two former neighbors since then. The prosecution objects to his reputation testimony. What is the best ruling?
o: Sustain, if he lacks enough acquaintance with the defendant and his community to speak with authority.
Overrule, because any personal acquaintance with the defendant qualifies a character witness to testify.
Overrule, because remoteness in time goes only to the weight of reputation testimony, never admissibility.
Sustain, because after a witness moves away only opinion testimony, not reputation, is permitted.
oe: Correct. This is the Michelson foundation standard; Whitmore applied similar remoteness concerns to 608(a) witnesses.
The witness must know the reputation in the relevant community at about the time of trial.
Courts exclude for inadequate foundation (Whitmore).
Opinion also needs an adequate basis; moving away doesn't convert the form.
pre: A defendant charged with wire fraud calls a neighbor who testifies to the defendant's excellent reputation for honesty. On direct, defense counsel also asks the neighbor to describe the time the defendant returned a lost wallet with $500 in it. On cross, the prosecutor, who has a police report, asks, “Have you heard that in 2016 he was arrested for check-kiting?” Which rulings are correct?

q: A defendant charged with assault claims self-defense and calls a witness to testify that the victim has a reputation for violence. The defendant offers no evidence of his own character. In rebuttal, the prosecution offers (1) a witness to the victim's reputation for peacefulness and (2) a witness to the defendant's reputation for violence. Which is admissible?
o: Both.
Only (1), because the defendant never put his own character in issue.
Only (2), because the victim's character isn't on trial.
Neither, because 404(a)(2)(B) is subject to Rule 412.
oe: Correct. When the accused offers the victim's pertinent trait, the prosecution may rebut it and may offer evidence of the accused's same trait (404(a)(2)(B)(i)–(ii), added in 2000).
(B)(ii) lets the prosecution offer the same trait in the defendant anyway, which had no common-law counterpart.
Rebutting the victim's trait is expressly permitted.
412 matters only in sexual-misconduct cases.

q: In a murder trial, the defendant offers no character evidence but testifies that the victim swung a bottle at him first. The prosecution then calls a witness to testify that the victim had a reputation for peacefulness. Would the result differ if the victim had survived and the charge were assault?
o: Yes; only in homicide may first-aggressor evidence alone trigger the victim's peacefulness.
No; the prosecution may offer the victim's peacefulness whenever the defendant claims self-defense.
No; the prosecution may never offer the victim's character unless the defense offers character first.
Yes; in an assault case the surviving victim may testify freely to his own peaceful nature.
oe: Correct. 404(a)(2)(C) is limited to homicide and is triggered by first-aggressor evidence of any kind.
Outside homicide, the defendant must first offer the victim's trait.
404(a)(2)(C) is the exception.
A victim's testimony about his own peacefulness is still character evidence subject to 404.

q: A defendant charged with assault claims self-defense. He offers testimony describing three specific bar fights the victim started years ago, none of which the defendant knew about. Under what theory, if any, is this admissible?
o: None as offered; the victim's character isn't an element of self-defense, so use 404(a)(2)(B) instead.
Under 405(b), because the victim's violent character is an essential element of a self-defense claim.
Under 404(b)(2), because the earlier fights show the victim's motive to attack the defendant.
Under 406, because starting three bar fights over several years shows a habit of violence.
oe: Correct. The slides tie this to James: what matters is the defendant's fear at the time. Had he known of the fights, they could come in to show his state of mind, a non-character use.
Courts reject that view; self-defense doesn't make character an element.
Fights years earlier don't show a motive in this encounter; it's propensity.
Violent fights aren't a semi-automatic, regular response; they're character.

q: Variation: In which case may character be proved by specific instances under 405(b)?
o: A drug case in which the defendant claims entrapment and the government offers prior sales.
A theft case in which the defendant offers specific instances of his honesty with money.
A negligence suit in which the plaintiff offers the defendant's record of careless driving.
A self-defense case in which the defendant offers the victim's specific violent acts.
oe: Correct. Predisposition is an element of the entrapment defense. Others include defamation (truth), negligent entrustment, custody, and sexually-violent-person commitments.
Honesty isn't an element of theft; 405(a) governs.
Careless character isn't an element of ordinary negligence. Contrast negligent entrustment, where the entrustee's incompetence is.
Covered by the prior question: not an essential element.
pre: A defendant charged with assault claims self-defense. He offers testimony describing three specific bar fights the victim started years ago, none of which the defendant knew about. Under what theory, if any, is this admissible?

q: Charged with shooting her neighbor, a defendant testifies, “I wouldn't shoot anybody.” The prosecutor asks on cross, “You've shot at people before, haven't you? You told detectives so.” The defense objects. What is the best analysis?
o: Likely permitted; she made herself a character witness and her prior statement impeaches her.
Barred, because the prosecution may never initiate evidence of the accused's character.
Barred, because specific instances of conduct may be proven only through extrinsic evidence.
Permitted, and the jury may use the past shootings as evidence that she shot the neighbor.
oe: Correct. That was the professor's analysis of Problem 3.16.
She opened the door by offering her own peaceful character.
Specific instances on cross are permitted; extrinsic proof is what's restricted.
The jury may use it to assess her claim and credibility, not as propensity.
topic: Character evidence — Defendant as character witness

q: In a civil fraud suit, the defendant calls a witness to testify that the plaintiff, who testified, has a bad reputation for truthfulness. The plaintiff objects that 404(a)(2) applies only in criminal cases. How should the court rule?
o: Overrule; 404(a)(3) allows witness truthfulness under 607–609 in civil and criminal cases.
Sustain; character evidence is never admissible in civil cases under the 2006 amendment.
Sustain; only the plaintiff herself may put her character for truthfulness in issue.
Overrule, but only because the plaintiff first offered evidence of her own good character.
oe: Correct. Witness-character rules apply in both kinds of cases, unlike 404(a)(2).
404(a)(3) and 608 apply in civil cases.
Under 608 either party may initiate a character attack on a witness's truthfulness.
608(a) allows the attack without any prior opening.

q: A defendant's character witness testifies, “In my own opinion, based on twenty years as his business partner, he is scrupulously honest.” The prosecutor objects that at common law character could be shown only by reputation, and that any reputation evidence is hearsay. What is the best ruling?
o: Overrule; 405(a) permits opinion, and reputation is admitted as hearsay under 803(21).
Sustain; the Federal Rules codified the common law's rule that only reputation may be offered.
Sustain; a witness's personal opinion of character is speculation and never admissible.
Overrule; character evidence is entirely exempt from the hearsay rules.
oe: Correct. The FRE departed from the common law (which allowed only reputation) by adding opinion.
405(a) allows either form.
Lay opinion about character is expressly allowed.
Reputation is hearsay, admitted through a specific exception.

q: A worker is injured when a can of refrigerant explodes. He sues the manufacturer, testifying that he warmed the can in a bucket of warm water. The manufacturer offers coworkers who saw him heat cans with an induction coil (which would make him at fault). Which testimony best qualifies as habit?
o: A coworker who saw him use the coil dozens of times over two years.
A coworker who saw him use the coil once, the week before the explosion.
A coworker who will say he is generally careless with all of his equipment.
None, because habit evidence is admissible only with corroboration.
oe: Correct. Halloran v. Virginia Chemicals allowed habit evidence on such facts if the conduct is regular and repeated: “predictable and predictive,” like buckling a seatbelt.
Occasional conduct isn't habit.
General carelessness is character, not habit.
406 admits habit regardless of corroboration or an eyewitness.

q: A federal physician is charged with sexually abusing two patients during exams. The government gives timely notice that it will offer four other women who say he abused them in similar exams. The defense argues the case would require dueling experts on medical propriety for every incident. The trial court excludes the four women under 403. On appeal, what is the likely result?
o: Affirmed; the threshold is met, but ordinary 403 applies and a six-incident trial justified exclusion.
Reversed, because Rule 413 evidence must be admitted once its three-part threshold is satisfied.
Reversed, because 403 must be applied with a strong presumption in favor of admitting 413 evidence.
Affirmed, because other sexual assaults are admissible only if they resulted in convictions.
oe: Correct. Guardia affirmed on these facts under abuse-of-discretion review.
413 says the court “may” admit (restyled in 2011 from “is admissible”), and 403 applies.
Guardia said courts should not alter their normal 403 weighing.
No conviction is needed; the standard is presumably 104(b)/Huddleston.

q: In a federal child-molestation prosecution, the government offers the defendant's uncharged molestation of another child under Rule 414. The defendant argues that (1) the rule violates due process by letting jurors convict him for who he is, and (2) the Indiana Supreme Court abandoned this kind of exception in Lannan v. State. What is the best response?
o: Courts uphold 413/414 because 403 still screens the evidence; Lannan was a state case decided before them.
The rule is unconstitutional, because a ban on propensity evidence is required by due process.
Lannan controls, because it persuasively rejected both the recidivism rationale and the bolstering rationale for propensity evidence.
The evidence is admissible only if offered for a 404(b)(2) purpose such as common plan.
oe: Correct. In Mound, Judge Richard Arnold rejected the challenge; his brother Judge Morris Arnold dissented from denial of rehearing en banc. Lannan adopted 404(b) in Indiana in 1992.
No court has so held; the dissent argued only that the question deserved consideration.
Lannan was a state-law decision; Congress later enacted 413–415.
414 allows propensity use directly.

q: A woman sues a businessman for battery, alleging he sexually assaulted her in a department-store dressing room. She gives notice that she will call two other women who say he assaulted them, and will play a recording of him boasting about grabbing women. He objects that this is propensity evidence. What is the best ruling?
o: Admissible under 415 to show his propensity, subject to 403.
Inadmissible, because propensity exceptions apply only in criminal prosecutions.
Admissible only if the other women's allegations led to criminal convictions.
Inadmissible, because Rule 415 covers only claims of child molestation.
oe: Correct. Carroll v. Trump (S.D.N.Y. 2023) admitted similar evidence under 415, noting it was offered to show propensity.
415 applies 413 and 414 to civil cases.
No conviction is required.
415 covers sexual assault and child molestation.

q: A law student summarizes the legislative background of Rules 413–415. Which statement is accurate?
o: No conviction is needed; the Judicial Conference opposed the rules; Baker cited low sex-offense rearrest rates.
The Judicial Conference drafted the rules, and Congress adopted the Conference's text without change.
The rules require the prosecution to prove the other sexual assaults beyond a reasonable doubt.
Congress acted because state courts had uniformly admitted propensity evidence in sex-offense cases.
oe: Correct. Molinari's floor statement, the Judicial Conference's 1995 report, and Baker's critique are the main sources discussed in Class 7.
Congress enacted them in 1994; the Conference opposed them in 1995.
The standard is presumably 104(b)'s sufficiency test.
States were split; Indiana (Lannan) and New Hampshire (Kirsch) rejected such evidence.

q: Police find a bag of methamphetamine under the passenger seat of the defendant's car. He testifies he thought the bag held vitamins. Before trial, the prosecutor gave written notice that she would offer his two-year-old conviction for selling methamphetamine, explaining it shows he would recognize the drug. What is the best analysis?
o: Admissible for knowledge if it survives 403, with a limiting instruction on request.
Inadmissible, because prior drug crimes are always propensity evidence in a drug case.
Admissible to show he is a drug dealer and therefore likely possessed the drugs.
Inadmissible, because notice must be given when the evidence is offered, not before trial.
oe: Correct. Notice under 404(b)(3) was given with the purpose and reasoning. Critics warn knowledge theories can slide into propensity, so the 403 weighing matters.
Knowledge is a permitted purpose when the chain avoids character.
That's the forbidden propensity chain.
404(b)(3) requires reasonable written notice before trial (or during trial for good cause).
topic: Other acts (404(b)) — Knowledge · chain test · notice

q: A man is charged with selling 5,000 stolen videotapes. To prove he knew they were stolen, the government offers evidence that a few months earlier he sold 38 new televisions far below market price and couldn't produce a bill of sale. He was tried for stealing the televisions and acquitted. What standard governs admission?
o: Whether a jury could reasonably find the TVs were stolen; the acquittal doesn't bar the evidence.
The judge must find by clear and convincing evidence that the televisions were in fact stolen.
The acquittal bars any use of the televisions as evidence of the defendant's knowledge.
The judge must find under Rule 104(a), by a preponderance, that the televisions were stolen.
oe: Correct. Huddleston applied 104(b) to other acts, finding low price, large quantity and no bill of sale sufficient. Dowling held acquitted conduct may be used.
Huddleston rejected heightened standards.
Dowling rejected that argument.
Huddleston held no 104(a) finding is required.

q: A car bomb kills a police officer. The bomb was remote-controlled, radio-activated, built from hobby-store parts with an unusual fusing circuit, and placed to benefit a friend of the builder. The defendant previously built a bomb with the same features, also for a friend. In a separate case, a robbery defendant's only similarity to an earlier robbery is that both robbers used a knife. Which other-act evidence is admissible to prove identity?
o: The earlier bomb, if it passes 403; the knife robbery isn't admissible, because a knife isn't a signature.
Both, because each shows the defendant previously committed a crime similar to the one charged.
Neither, because identity can never be proven by evidence of a defendant's other crimes.
The knife robbery only, because weapons evidence is more probative than bomb-construction methods.
oe: Correct. Trenkler's two-part test asks for special relevance beyond propensity, then 403. Pisari reversed where the only similarity was a knife.
Similarity alone without a signature is propensity.
Identity is a recognized 404(b)(2) purpose when a signature exists.
A knife is a generic feature; the bomb's design is distinctive.

q: Variation: The earlier bomb caused no injuries. A database search found only 7 of 40,867 incidents shared the queried features. What did the Trenkler dissent argue?
o: The database query was skewed, and the two bombs differed fundamentally in design.
The earlier bomb was inadmissible because the defendant was never charged for it.
Identity wasn't actually disputed, so the earlier bomb was irrelevant to any issue.
The defendant's stipulation to the earlier bomb required the court to exclude it.
oe: Correct. The majority admitted the evidence because the earlier bomb caused no injuries, so a limiting instruction sufficed.
Uncharged acts may be used under 404(b).
Identity was the central issue.
He stipulated he built it; that made it easier to admit.
pre: A car bomb kills a police officer. The bomb was remote-controlled, radio-activated, built from hobby-store parts with an unusual fusing circuit, and placed to benefit a friend of the builder. The defendant previously built a bomb with the same features, also for a friend. In a separate case, a robbery defendant's only similarity to an earlier robbery is that both robbers used a knife. Which other-act evidence is admissible to prove identity?

q: A prosecutor is murdered in her apartment, with no sign of forced entry. At the trial of her colleague, the prosecution asks their supervisor whether the defendant and the victim had an affair. The defense objects that he's on trial for murder, not adultery. What is the best ruling?
o: Admissible for motive and opportunity unless unfair prejudice substantially outweighs it, which is unlikely.
Inadmissible, because the question assumes a fact that hasn't yet been proven in evidence.
Inadmissible, because an affair is a bad act that is being offered to show immoral character.
Admissible, but only after the defense first offers evidence of the defendant's good character and so opens the door to rebuttal.
oe: Correct. That was the analysis of the Presumed Innocent clip. The defense's better objection is unfair prejudice, but an affair is probative of motive.
Questions can introduce evidence; the prosecutor needn't ask only about facts already proved.
It's offered for motive and opportunity, not character.
404(b) purposes don't require the defense to open the door.
topic: Other acts (404(b)) — Motive & opportunity · Presumed Innocent

q: Variation: In a civil suit, a television-studio employee knocked over a child while racing down a hallway. The plaintiff offers testimony that she was seen sprinting recklessly just seconds after the collision. The defense objects that this shows only a careless character. What is the best response?
o: It shows she was rushing at that moment to meet a deadline, not a careless character.
Evidence of a party's careless character is admissible in civil cases, where the 404 ban doesn't apply.
It is habit evidence under Rule 406, showing how she routinely moves.
It is inadmissible, because conduct after the collision is irrelevant.
oe: Correct. That was the Broadcast News clip analysis. The evidence is about the occasion itself.
404(a)(1) applies in civil cases.
One episode isn't a habit.
Conduct seconds later bears on her state of mind during the incident.
pre: A prosecutor is murdered in her apartment, with no sign of forced entry. At the trial of her colleague, the prosecution asks their supervisor whether the defendant and the victim had an affair. The defense objects that he's on trial for murder, not adultery. What is the best ruling?

q: A defendant is charged with a February hack of a retailer's customer database. The prosecution offers evidence that he hacked the same database in March using the same exploit. Separately, in a civil suit against a railroad, the plaintiff offers evidence that the engineer had twice been caught drinking on duty and the railroad was told. Which is the best analysis?
o: The hack may show know-how if it narrows the pool; the drinking may show the railroad's notice.
Both are barred as propensity evidence, because each shows a person's other wrongful acts.
The hack is admissible as propensity, because hacking is a specialized and unusual crime.
The drinking incidents may be used to prove the engineer was drunk on the day of the crash.
oe: Correct. Problem 3.1 (Hacker) is a knowledge route that depends on how rare the skill is. The railroad's notice is the railroad's knowledge, not the engineer's propensity.
Each has a non-character chain.
Specialized crimes are still covered by 404(b)(1) when offered for propensity.
That would be propensity.
topic: Other acts (404(b)) — Knowledge · Hacker · notice to employer

q: A defendant is charged with possessing a revolver with an obliterated serial number. He claims it belonged to his cousin. His girlfriend will testify she saw him load the revolver, spin the cylinder, put it to his head, and pull the trigger, a game he called “Russian roulette.” What is the best ruling?
o: Allow her to describe his handling and loading of the gun, but bar the “Russian roulette” label.
Exclude the whole account, because it portrays a reckless character and invites propensity reasoning.
Admit everything, because evidence that completes the story of the crime isn't subject to Rule 403.
Exclude it unless she also saw him with the gun on the day the police found it.
oe: Correct. In Hite the court kept the account coherent but sanitized the label to reduce unfair prejudice.
His handling of the gun is directly probative of possession.
403 always applies; Stephens even called res gestae obsolete in federal law.
Earlier possession is still probative.

q: A man's third wife drowns in the bathtub soon after making a will in his favor. He says she fainted. The prosecution offers evidence that his first two wives also drowned in their bathtubs shortly after making wills naming him. What is the best analysis?
o: Admissible to show absence of accident, though scholars debate whether it avoids propensity.
Inadmissible, because the earlier deaths were never charged or proven in any court.
Admissible to show that he is a murderous type of person who kills for money.
Inadmissible unless he was convicted of causing the deaths of his first and second wives in earlier prosecutions.
oe: Correct. Rex v. Smith (Brides in the Bath). Imwinkelried says the reasoning focuses on objective improbability; critics say it still asks how likely an innocent man is to be so often unlucky.
Uncharged acts can be used under 404(b).
That's the forbidden inference.
Huddleston's sufficiency standard applies, not conviction.

q: In a state that follows the federal rules but has no counterpart to Rules 413–415, a church youth leader is charged with molesting a girl. The prosecution offers evidence that he molested three other girls from the church in similar ways, arguing it shows motive, intent, and a common plan. How did State v. Kirsch treat similar arguments?
o: It rejected all three: motive and intent were propensity in disguise, and a pattern isn't a plan.
It admitted them under common plan, because using similar methods with several girls shows a plan.
It admitted them under Rule 413, because the charged crime was a sexual offense against a child.
It admitted them for intent, because intent is always genuinely at issue in sexual-assault cases.
oe: Correct. Kirsch is a rare court recognizing that 404(b)(2) purposes aren't exceptions to the propensity bar.
A systematic course of conduct is insufficient for a plan.
The state had no 413 counterpart.
The intent theory collapsed into propensity.
topic: Other acts (404(b)) — Common plan vs. pattern · Kirsch

q: A defendant charged with a gunpoint robbery at a military base offers testimony from another victim, robbed nearby the same week in a similar way, who says the defendant was not his attacker. In a different case, a felon-in-possession defendant offers his co-arrestee's prior gun conviction to suggest the gun was the co-arrestee's. Which is the better candidate for admission?
o: The other victim's testimony, which supports a same-perpetrator inference under 401 and survives 403.
The co-arrestee's conviction, because defendants may offer any propensity evidence about third parties.
Neither, because Rule 404(b) doesn't apply to evidence offered by criminal defendants.
Both, because unfair prejudice to the government is never a factor in the 403 balance.
oe: Correct. Stevens applied a lower similarity threshold for defense evidence (no signature required). Williams rejected a pure propensity use.
Reverse 404(b) isn't a license for propensity.
It applies to any person; the standard is more relaxed when no prejudice to the defendant is at stake.
The government can claim unfair prejudice; Stevens simply found little risk here.

q: At a murder trial, the prosecution offers violent rap lyrics the defendant wrote years earlier about shooting rivals, with no reference to the victim, the location, or the details of the charged shooting. Under the cases and statutes covered in class, what is the best assessment?
o: Likely excluded absent a specific link to the crime, though closely matching lyrics might show intent.
Admissible as a confession, because the defendant wrote the lyrics in the first person.
Inadmissible in all cases under a federal statute that bars lyrics as evidence of guilt.
Admissible to show motive, because violent lyrics written by a defendant always reveal what the writer has in mind.
oe: Correct. State v. Skinner (N.J.) condemned such lyrics and affirmed reversal; Bey-Cousin v. Powell presumed lyrics are fiction. California, Louisiana and Maryland statutes make creative expression harder to admit, without an absolute bar.
First-person narration isn't a confession (Bey-Cousin's Johnny Cash example).
No federal statute has passed.
That's propensity unless tied to the specific crime.

q: A cyclist sues a competitor over a racing crash, and the defendant offers brochures the plaintiff recently published for bicycle-racing equipment, to show he is an experienced racer who knew the risks. The plaintiff objects under 404(b)(1). What is the best assessment?
o: Technically within 404(b)(1), but racing bikes poses little risk of unfair prejudice.
It must be excluded, because 404(b)(1) covers any “act,” bad or innocent.
It is admissible as habit evidence under Rule 406, because he races regularly and predictably.
It is admissible only under 405(b), as an essential element.
oe: Correct. That was the professor's view of Problem 3.9: 404 targets prejudicial propensity, not innocuous activity.
That's the literal reading the analysis cautions against.
Publishing brochures isn't a semi-automatic habit.
Character isn't an element here.

q: In a California murder trial, a prosecutor offers a former girlfriend's testimony that the defendant repeatedly threatened her during their relationship, under California Evidence Code § 1109. If the same case were tried in federal court, what would be the most likely result?
o: Likely excluded; the FRE have no domestic-violence propensity exception like § 1109.
Admissible under Rule 413, because domestic violence is a form of sexual assault.
Admissible under 404(a)(2)(C), because the victim of the charged crime was killed.
Admissible under Rule 406, as evidence of a habit of threatening his partners.
oe: Correct. § 1109 lets California admit prior domestic violence in DV prosecutions. The federal rules' only true propensity exceptions are 413–415 (plus 404(a)(2)–(3)).
413 is limited to sexual assault as defined.
(C) concerns the victim's peacefulness, not the defendant's other acts.
Threats aren't a semi-automatic habit.

q: A defendant is charged with shooting two federal agents who approached his vehicle. The prosecution, after giving proper notice, offers evidence that he knew a warrant had issued for his arrest on an unrelated attempted-murder charge. The defense objects that this tells the jury he's a violent criminal. What is the best ruling?
o: Admissible for motive, subject to 403 and a limiting instruction.
Inadmissible, because evidence of another pending charge is always propensity.
Admissible to show he is a violent person likely to shoot officers.
Inadmissible unless he was convicted of the attempted-murder charge.
oe: Correct. This is the Peltier pattern: the inference runs through motive, not character.
The warrant's relevance comes from its effect on his motive.
That's the barred use; the limiting instruction should forbid it.
Conviction isn't required; his knowledge of the warrant is what matters.

q: In a civil collision case, the plaintiff calls an eyewitness expecting her to say the defendant ran a red light. Instead she testifies the light was green. Plaintiff's counsel wants to (1) show she told a police officer at the scene that the light was red, and (2) show she wasn't wearing her prescription glasses that day. Which is correct?
o: Both are permitted; 607 lets the calling party impeach its own witness on either theory.
Neither is permitted, because a party vouches for the credibility of the witnesses it calls.
Only the glasses evidence, because a prior inconsistent statement is a character-based attack.
Only the prior statement, because poor eyesight goes to weight and isn't impeachment at all.
oe: Correct. Neither theory runs through character, so 608 and 609 don't control.
Rule 607 abolished that limit.
A prior inconsistent statement generally goes around the propensity box.
Showing a witness is honestly mistaken is a recognized mode of impeachment.

q: On cross, the prosecutor asks the defendant's alibi witness, “Didn't you claim on a bank loan application that you had no debt, when you owed $82,000 in student loans?” He answers, “No.” She then asks, “Aren't you in business with the defendant's father?” He answers, “No.” The prosecutor wants to call (1) the loan officer to prove the false application and (2) a business partner to prove the partnership. Which may she call?
o: Only the business partner.
Only the loan officer, because a false loan application is highly probative of untruthfulness.
Both, because the witness denied each fact and the prosecutor may prove what he denied.
Neither, because a witness's answers on cross-examination are binding on the examiner.
oe: Correct. 608(b) bars extrinsic evidence of specific acts offered to show untruthful character, so she must take the answer about the loan. Bias is never collateral and may be proved extrinsically (Abel; Problem 4.8).
Probative or not, 608(b) forbids extrinsic proof.
The denial doesn't open the door to extrinsic proof under 608(b).
Only the 608(b) answer is binding; bias may be proved.

q: In a civil real-estate dispute, the plaintiff testifies. The defense then calls a witness who says, “Her reputation in town is terrible,” and is about to add that the plaintiff belongs to a fringe religious group that “doesn't believe in oaths.” What should the court do?
o: Sustain both objections; a question limited to reputation for truthfulness would be allowed.
Allow both, because a party who testifies opens her entire character to attack by the opponent.
Allow the reputation testimony but bar the religious comment, since only 610 limits the attack.
Bar both, because Rule 608(a) applies only to witnesses in criminal prosecutions.
oe: Correct. That was the Easerly v. Lettwin clip: “terrible reputation” is too broad. 608(a) reaches any testifying witness in civil and criminal cases.
Testifying exposes only her character for truthfulness, through the 608/609 channels.
General reputation isn't limited to truthfulness.
608 applies in both civil and criminal cases.

q: A police officer is the only witness tying the defendant to a gun. The defense offers (1) a reporter who wrote an article about the officer's dishonesty three years before trial; (2) a defense lawyer who says the officer has a bad reputation in the “court community” after talking with a few colleagues; and (3) cross-examination asking the officer whether his driver's license was suspended and he failed to report it as required, based on a motor-vehicle record that is itself hearsay. The trial judge excludes all three, and the jury convicts. On appeal, what result is most likely?
o: No abuse as to the character witnesses; reversible error as to the cross, which needed only a good-faith basis.
Affirmance on all three, because the motor-vehicle record supporting the cross was inadmissible hearsay.
Reversal on all three, because a defendant has a constitutional right to present any impeachment he chooses.
Error as to the reporter only, because journalists are always qualified to testify about reputation.
oe: Correct. That's Whitmore: the record supplied a reasonable basis, counsel would be bound by the answer, and the court couldn't assume the officer would lie.
The record needn't be admissible; it only supplies the good-faith basis for asking.
The 608(a) exclusions were within the trial court's discretion.
Remoteness in time defeated the reporter's foundation.

q: In an employment suit, the plaintiff (a lawyer) testifies. On cross, defense counsel asks (1) whether he visited an adult movie theater, and (2) whether he falsely stated on his bar application that he had no unpaid parking tickets. In a separate criminal case, a prosecutor asks a defense witness whether she once falsely reported being kidnapped; when the defense objects that there's “no proof,” the prosecutor offers the witness's affidavit admitting the lie. Which ruling is correct?
o: Question (2) and the kidnapping question are proper; question (1) and the affidavit are not.
All of them are proper, because a testifying witness's credibility is always at issue in the case.
Only question (1) is proper, because visiting an adult theater shows the plaintiff's immorality.
None of them are proper, because specific instances of conduct may never be raised on cross.
oe: Correct. 608(b) acts must be probative of truthfulness: immorality isn't, lying in a semi-official setting is. The questioner needs a good-faith basis, not proof, and can't prove the act extrinsically, so the affidavit is out.
Specific acts must bear on truthfulness, and extrinsic proof is barred.
Immorality isn't untruthfulness (Philadelphia clip).
608(b) expressly allows them on cross.
topic: Impeachment — 608(b) probative of truthfulness · good faith

q: A defense witness is impeached with his six-year-old armed-robbery conviction under 609(a)(1)(A). The defense then calls his neighbor, who testifies that in her opinion he is truthful. On cross, the prosecutor asks the neighbor, “Did you know he lied on a loan application about $82,000 in student debt?” Is the sequence proper?
o: Yes; the conviction opened the door to support, and 608(b)(2) allows the question to the neighbor.
No, because rehabilitation is allowed only after an attack by opinion or reputation under 608(a).
No, because a character witness may never be cross-examined about the principal witness's acts.
Yes, and if the neighbor denies knowing of it, the prosecutor may call the loan officer to prove it.
oe: Correct. That's Problem 4.6(4): the question tests whether her opinion is well informed.
Attacks under 608(a), 608(b) and 609 all open the door.
608(b)(2) permits it.
Extrinsic proof of the act is still barred.

q: Four defense witnesses are cross-examined. Witness 1 admits he is in business with the defendant's father. Witness 2 concedes one detail was wrong (the deli was closed that day, so they ate next door). Witness 3 admits lying on a loan application. Witness 4 is impeached with a prior perjury conviction. The defense then offers testimony to each witness's good reputation for truthfulness. For which witnesses is it admissible?
o: Witnesses 3 and 4.
All four, because each witness's credibility was attacked on cross-examination.
Only Witness 4, because only prior convictions attack character for truthfulness.
Witnesses 1, 3 and 4, because bias is itself a form of untruthfulness.
oe: Correct. Bias isn't an attack on character for truthfulness (ACN 608(a)), and a single contradiction isn't either (Problem 4.6). 608(b) acts and 609 convictions are character attacks.
Only character attacks open the door under 608(a).
608(b) acts do too.
The Advisory Committee's Note says bias is not a character attack.
topic: Impeachment — What opens the door to rehabilitation

q: In a benefits-fraud trial, the victim is the government's key witness. Defense counsel says in opening that she is “receiving government benefits again” and was recently cleared in her own investigation, and asks her on cross whether her payments are tied to testifying. The government then calls two witnesses to her honesty. Separately, in another trial, a prosecutor calls a witness's pastor to vouch for her honesty before any cross-examination. Which is correct?
o: The pastor's testimony is impermissible bolstering, and Bonner's ruling is debatable because the attacks went to bias.
Both are proper, because a party may always offer evidence supporting the honesty of its key witness.
Both are improper, because an opening statement can never constitute an attack on a witness's credibility.
The pastor's testimony is proper because it came before cross, when the witness's credibility was not yet in doubt.
oe: Correct. Bolstering before any attack is barred. In Bonner the attacks suggested a motive to lie, which the ACN to 608(a) says is not a character attack.
Support is allowed only after a character attack.
The issue isn't the timing of the attack but its nature (bias).
That's exactly what bolstering is.

q: In an intersection-crash trial, a witness testifies that the light was green and that a car parked across the street was red. The defense calls (1) a witness who says the light was red, and (2) a witness who says the parked car was blue, offered only to show the first witness's poor perception. Under modern practice, which is correct?
o: (1) is admissible; (2) is collateral and now decided under 403; cross on the car's color is always allowed.
Both are barred, because extrinsic evidence may never be offered to contradict a witness's testimony.
Both are admissible as of right, because contradicting a witness's testimony is never collateral.
(2) is admissible only under Rule 608(b), as a specific instance probative of untruthfulness.
oe: Correct. Extrinsic evidence on collateral matters is now a 403 question, and cross-examination isn't extrinsic evidence.
Contradiction on material facts is ordinary evidence.
Collateral contradiction is subject to 403.
Contradiction isn't a 608(b) specific-act inquiry.

q: Variation: The defense contradicts the witness on four separate points and argues in closing that, having been wrong or untruthful on all four, she can't be believed about anything. May the proponent now offer evidence of her good character for truthfulness?
o: Possibly; whether contradiction attacks character depends on the circumstances, and pervasive contradiction may.
No, because contradiction is never an attack on a witness's character for truthfulness, however extensive.
Yes, automatically, whenever opposing counsel contradicts the witness on at least one point.
No, because rehabilitation is permitted only after impeachment with a prior conviction under 609.
oe: Correct. A single contradiction isn't an attack, but pervasive contradiction offered to show general untruthfulness may be.
The ACN leaves room for pervasive contradiction.
One contradiction doesn't open the door (Problem 4.6).
608(a) and 608(b) attacks also open the door.
topic: Impeachment — When contradiction becomes a character attack

q: In a federal criminal trial, four convictions are offered to impeach four different witnesses, none more than ten years old. Which must be admitted with no balancing at all?
o: A prosecution witness's misdemeanor conviction for making a false statement.
The defendant's felony conviction for armed robbery committed with a handgun.
A defense witness's felony conviction for possession with intent to distribute drugs.
A prosecution witness's misdemeanor conviction for petty theft from a store.
oe: Correct. 609(a)(2) requires admission of any crime whose elements required a dishonest act or false statement, for any witness and regardless of punishment. Such convictions are “peculiarly probative” and “always to be admitted.”
Robbery isn't crimen falsi; for the accused, 609(a)(1)(B) requires that probative value outweigh prejudice.
609(a)(1)(A): admitted subject to 403, so balancing applies.
Not crimen falsi and not a felony, so not admissible under 609 at all.

q: Variation: A jailhouse informant testifies for the prosecution. He pleaded guilty last month to felony arson but hasn't been sentenced, spent time in reform school as a teenager, and has a five-year-old petty-larceny conviction (maximum six months). Which may the defense use to impeach him?
o: The arson conviction, subject to 403, but not the reform school or the petty larceny.
None, because he hasn't yet been sentenced for the arson he pleaded guilty to.
All three, because an informant may be impeached with any prior wrongdoing.
Only the larceny, because every theft offense involves dishonesty.
oe: Correct. “Punishable by” refers to the possible sentence, not the one imposed. 609(d) allows a witness's juvenile adjudication only if necessary to fairly determine guilt. Larceny generally isn't crimen falsi (Anatomy of a Murder clip).
The possible punishment controls.
609's categories still apply.
Theft and larceny generally aren't crimen falsi.
pre: In a federal criminal trial, four convictions are offered to impeach four different witnesses, none more than ten years old. Which must be admitted with no balancing at all?

q: A defendant charged with transporting a stolen vehicle will testify. The government seeks to impeach him with prior convictions for kidnapping, rape, aggravated assault, and assault with a deadly weapon; he committed several of them while on parole. Credibility is central because his testimony directly contradicts the government's witnesses. Applying the Gordon factors, which statement is correct?
o: Violence cuts against admission, but his continuing record and central credibility cut for it; some may come in.
All four must be excluded, because violent crimes never bear on a witness's truthfulness.
All four must be admitted, because each crime was punishable by more than a year in prison and is therefore a qualifying felony.
The more similar a prior is to the charged crime, the more probative and admissible it becomes.
oe: Correct. That's Brewer, which excluded the kidnapping conviction as “overkill” and admitted the other three. More violent means less probative of honesty; factors 4 and 5 often counterbalance.
Gordon says they have little direct bearing, but the other factors can favor admission.
For the accused, 609(a)(1)(B) requires weighing.
Similarity increases prejudice (“he did it before”) and weighs against admission.

q: A defendant testifies at his 2026 trial. He was convicted of armed robbery in 2013 and released from prison in 2018. Which standard governs the government's use of the conviction?
o: 609(a)(1)(B), because fewer than ten years have passed since his release from prison.
609(b), because more than ten years have passed since the date of his conviction.
609(a)(2), because robbery is a crime involving dishonesty and must be admitted.
Rule 403 alone, because he is the defendant and his testimony is central to the case.
oe: Correct. The ten years run from the later of conviction or release. Brewer applied the same release-date analysis.
Release, the later date, controls.
Robbery isn't crimen falsi.
(a)(1)(A)'s 403 standard applies to witnesses other than the accused.

q: Variation: He was released in 2014. What must the government show?
o: Probative value, backed by specific facts, must substantially outweigh prejudice, plus written notice.
Only that the conviction's probative value outweighs its prejudicial effect on the defendant.
Nothing more than the conviction itself, because the crime was a felony when committed.
That the defendant has committed no other crimes in the years since he was released.
oe: Correct. 609(b) is a “reverse 403” test; such convictions come in “very rarely and only in exceptional circumstances.”
That's the (a)(1)(B) standard, superseded by 609(b) here.
Age changes the standard.
That's relevant under Gordon factor 2, not a 609(b) requirement.
pre: A defendant testifies at his 2026 trial. He was convicted of armed robbery in 2013 and released from prison in 2018. Which standard governs the government's use of the conviction?

q: In a federal criminal trial, which of these may be used to impeach?
o: A prosecution witness's juvenile adjudication, if an adult conviction would be admissible and it's necessary.
The defendant's own juvenile adjudication for perjury, because perjury is always crimen falsi.
A witness's felony conviction that was later pardoned on a finding that the witness was innocent.
A witness's conviction set aside by a certificate of rehabilitation, with no felony committed since.
oe: Correct. 609(d) allows a juvenile adjudication only in a criminal case, against a witness other than the defendant, under those two conditions.
609(d) never allows juvenile adjudications against the accused.
609(c)(2) bars convictions set aside on a finding of innocence.
609(c)(1) bars it.

q: Before trial, the judge rules that if the defendant testifies, the government may impeach him with a prior drug-distribution conviction, which the government will identify by name. Defense counsel is considering three options: (1) don't testify and appeal the ruling; (2) testify and bring out the conviction on direct to “draw the sting”; (3) testify and let the government raise it on cross. Which option preserves the issue for appeal?
o: Only option (3).
Option (1), because a pretrial ruling on admissibility is final and reviewable.
Option (2), because it shows the jury the defendant has nothing to hide.
Options (2) and (3), because in both the conviction comes before the jury.
oe: Correct. Luce requires the defendant to testify to preserve the claim, and Ohler holds that bringing the conviction out yourself waives it. Courts usually let jurors learn the crime's name (Estrada).
Luce: without testimony the appellate court can't assess the harm.
Ohler: drawing the sting waives the objection.
Only the government's introduction preserves it.

q: In a cocaine-distribution trial, the judge excludes the defendant's prior cocaine conviction from the government's case-in-chief under 404(b) and 403. The defendant then testifies, and the government offers the same conviction under 609(a)(1)(B). The defendant argues the earlier exclusion dictates exclusion now. What is the best response?
o: The tests differ: one weighs proof of guilt, the other truthfulness against prejudice, so the earlier ruling isn't binding.
The earlier ruling is binding as the law of the case and governs any later offer of the same conviction.
Rule 609 always admits a conviction that was excluded under 404(b), because by choosing to testify the defendant put his credibility in issue.
The two tests are identical in substance, so the conviction must again be excluded.
oe: Correct. Valencia (8th Cir.) held the two weighings are separate (Problem 4.4).
It was a different test for a different purpose.
609(a)(1)(B) still requires probative value to outweigh prejudice.
They differ in both the probative value considered and the standard.

q: A witness has a misdemeanor conviction (maximum six months) under a statute punishing anyone who “tampers with, bypasses, or falsifies the reading of” a utility meter. Only one of those forms clearly involves deception. May it be used under 609(a)(2)?
o: Only if the court can readily tell it required deceit, looking to the indictment, admitted facts or instructions.
Yes, because any crime involving a utility meter is crimen falsi as a matter of law.
Yes, under 609(a)(1), because it is a misdemeanor punishable by up to six months.
No, because the court may consider only the name and elements of the statute of conviction, never the underlying record or plea.
oe: Correct. The 2006 ACN allows those sources. Tampering with a fact-recording meter arguably is deceit, and the 609(b) ten-year limit applies even to crimen falsi.
The court must be able to readily determine the dishonesty element.
609(a)(1) requires a crime punishable by more than one year.
The ACN allows the indictment, admitted facts, and jury instructions.
topic: Prior convictions (609) — Crimen falsi from the record · Problem 4.5

q: A defense lawyer with a client who has a prior felony is deciding whether the client should testify in a close case. Which empirical finding discussed in class bears most directly on the decision?
o: In weak cases, a known record can more than double the conviction rate, and jurors use priors for guilt.
Juries learn of a defendant's record just as often whether or not the defendant chooses to testify.
Perjury convictions lower credibility ratings far more than other convictions, as Rule 609 assumes.
Prior convictions have no measurable effect on verdicts in close or weak cases.
oe: Correct. Eisenberg & Hans (300+ trials; 45% of defendants with records testified vs. 62% without) and Wissler & Saks support counsel's caution. Roberts argues 609 forces a choice between silence and devastating impeachment, a vestige of the common-law rule that felons couldn't testify at all.
52% of juries learned of the record when the defendant testified vs. 9% when he didn't.
Wissler & Saks found credibility ratings unchanged across priors, while convictions rose.
The opposite: the effect is strongest in close or weak cases.

q: In a federal sexual-assault prosecution in which the defendant claims consent, he gives timely notice of four items: (1) the complainant's prior consensual relationship with him; (2) evidence that another man was the source of semen found on her; (3) her reputation in her dorm as promiscuous; and (4) photos of the revealing clothes she often wore to parties. Which may be admitted under 412?
o: Items (1) and (2).
All four, because the defendant claims consent.
Only (1), because evidence about other men is always barred.
Items (1), (2) and (3), because reputation is proper under 405(a).
oe: Correct. 412(b)(1)(B) covers specific instances with the accused, offered to prove consent; (b)(1)(A) covers specific instances showing someone else was the source of physical evidence. Reputation and “predisposition” evidence are exactly what 412(a) bars.
412 exists to stop the common-law consent inference (the old 404(a)(2)(B) analog).
(b)(1)(A) allows source-of-semen evidence.
No criminal exception allows reputation evidence of sexual behavior.

q: A defendant charged with rape claims consent and argues the complainant invented the assault because her boyfriend, with whom she lived, saw her get out of the defendant's car. The trial court bars any mention of the cohabitation, even after the complainant testifies she lived with her mother. The boyfriend is the only corroborating witness. What is the best analysis?
o: Excluding it violated the Confrontation Clause, because it showed a motive to fabricate.
The exclusion was proper, because a complainant's living arrangements are sexual behavior.
The exclusion was proper, because Chambers lets the evidence rules override the defense.
The evidence is admissible only to show that she was likely to have consented.
oe: Correct. This is Olden v. Kentucky, building on Davis v. Alaska (cross about a witness's probation to show bias).
Even if so, the Constitution required admission for bias.
Chambers recognizes the right but says it may bow to legitimate interests; bias evidence of this strength prevails.
Its proper use is bias, not consent propensity.

q: A defendant charged with attempted rape wants to testify that (1) just before the encounter he made remarks about the complainant's sexual history with other men, which angered her, to complete “the whole story”; and (2) he believed she consented because he had heard of her reputation and past sexual acts. Under the cases studied, what is the most likely ruling?
o: Both are likely excluded under Stephens and Knox; the right to present a defense can yield to 412's purposes.
Both are admissible, because a defendant has a right to tell his whole story to the jury in his own words.
Only (1), because res gestae evidence completing the story of a crime has constitutional status.
Only (2), because a defendant's state of mind is always relevant to a claimed belief in consent.
oe: Correct. Chambers recognizes a right to present critical defense evidence, but it may bow to legitimate interests such as encouraging victims to report and protecting their privacy.
Stephens rejected that argument; the right to testify isn't unlimited.
Stephens said res gestae has no federal constitutional significance.
Knox rejected it on the facts; at least one court (Doe) has admitted such evidence, but it's the minority view.

q: In a child-molestation trial, the defense seeks to cross-examine a witness about the complainant's earlier accusation against her cousin, which the cousin's brother says she later admitted was “just joking.” The complainant and her mother deny any recantation. The trial judge holds a hearing, decides he doesn't believe the accusation was false, and bars the questions under the rape-shield statute. What is the best analysis?
o: Error; false accusations aren't sexual behavior, and the test is whether a reasonable jury could find falsity.
Proper, because the rape shield bars any evidence that touches on a complainant's sexual history.
Proper, because the judge must first be persuaded by a preponderance of the evidence that the earlier accusation was actually false.
Error, because evidence of any prior accusation is admissible whether or not it was false.
oe: Correct. State v. Smith (La. 1999) reversed on these facts because the case turned entirely on the complainant's credibility.
Allegations aren't behavior; the ACN to 412 agrees.
The judge doesn't decide credibility; the standard is sufficiency for a reasonable jury.
A true prior accusation has no impeachment value; falsity is the point.
topic: Rape shield (412) — Prior false accusations · State v. Smith

q: Variation: In a molestation case, the judge lets the defense show the complainant lied to her parents about “texting” a boy, but bars any mention that the messages were “sexting” or of their content. Is that a reasonable accommodation?
o: Yes; the lie bears on truthfulness under 608(b), while the sexual content stays shielded.
No, because any evidence that the complainant lied to her parents is barred by Rule 412.
No, because the defense must be allowed to reveal the content to show how serious the lie was.
Yes, because Rule 412 bars all evidence about a complainant's use of her phone.
oe: Correct. The ruling lets the defense make its credibility point without exposing shielded sexual content.
Lies aren't sexual behavior.
The court may limit the evidence to what's probative of untruthfulness.
412 concerns sexual behavior and predisposition, not phone use generally.
topic: Rape shield (412) — Texting vs. sexting · Problem 5.6

The trial judge holds a hearing, decides he doesn't believe the accusation was false, and bars the questions under the rape-shield statute. What is the best analysis?

q: A defendant is charged with enticing a minor to produce sexually explicit images. He wants to show generally that the boy initiated sexual conversations and sent images of himself to other men, arguing the images may have been produced for someone else. How did the Eighth Circuit rule in United States v. Walker?
o: It excluded the evidence as general conduct, not the specific instances the source exception requires.
It admitted the evidence under 412(b)(1)(A), holding that digital images are physical evidence.
It admitted the evidence under 412(b)(1)(C), holding that the Constitution required it.
It held that Rule 412 doesn't apply when the alleged victim is male.
oe: Correct. Open questions remain: whether digital images count as “physical evidence,” and whether “specific instances” means single acts or discrete acts as opposed to reputation.
The court didn't reach admission on that ground.
No constitutional ruling compelled admission.
412 applies to any victim of alleged sexual misconduct.

q: A woman sues a public official for sexual harassment and claims the incident damaged her reputation. The official's lawyer threatens to explore her sexual history, calling the case “a two-way street.” Under 412(b)(2), what may the defense do?
o: Only if it substantially outweighs harm and prejudice, and reputation only if she put it in controversy.
Anything at all, because Rule 412 protects only complainants in criminal prosecutions and doesn't reach civil harassment suits.
Her reputation freely, because she sued in part for damage to her reputation.
Nothing, because Rule 412 bars all evidence of sexual behavior in civil cases.
oe: Correct. That's Problem 5.9 (Jones v. Clinton). The rules treat the parties' histories differently for policy, privacy and probative reasons.
412 applies in civil cases with its own balancing test.
Even then, the reverse-balancing test applies.
412(b)(2) permits it in narrow circumstances.
topic: Rape shield (412) — 412(b)(2) civil · Jones v. Clinton

q: A defense lawyer in a federal sexual-assault case wants to offer evidence under a 412(b) exception. What must she do?
o: File a sealed written motion at least 14 days before trial, notify the victim, and have an in camera hearing.
Simply raise the issue at trial when the complainant takes the stand and the evidence becomes relevant.
Obtain the victim's written consent before offering any evidence under a 412(b) exception.
Proffer the evidence in open court so the jury understands the nature of the dispute.
oe: Correct. 412(c) sets out these steps, and the victim and parties have a right to attend and be heard.
Advance motion practice is required absent a court order.
Consent isn't required; the court decides.
The hearing is in camera, and the record sealed.

q: Under Harriett Galvin's proposed rule, which bars a complainant's consensual sexual conduct with others only “to support the inference that a person who has previously engaged in consensual sexual conduct is for that reason more likely to consent,” which item excluded under the federal rule would most likely be admissible?
o: The defendant's knowledge of her past, offered to show his own belief in consent.
Her reputation for promiscuity, offered to show that she probably consented.
Her past consensual sex with others, offered to show she is more likely to lie.
Her past conduct with others, offered to show that she consented this time.
oe: Correct. Galvin's 404(b)-style rule targets only the consent-propensity and unworthy-of-belief inferences; the defendant's state of mind is a different inference (compare Knox). Colb would respond that once she swears she didn't consent, propensity data loses value.
That's exactly the inference Galvin would still bar.
Galvin would bar the unworthy-of-belief inference too.
That's the core forbidden inference.

q: Variation: A student argues that a complainant's frequency of consensual sex on first dates is relevant to whether she consented on the date in question. What is Sherry Colb's best response?
o: Her sworn denial overwhelms propensity data, and active women are no likelier to accuse falsely.
The evidence is relevant to consent, but it is always unfairly prejudicial under Rule 403.
The evidence becomes admissible if the defendant knew of her dating history beforehand.
Sexual history bears on a complainant's credibility, as Wigmore argued, so it should come in.
oe: Correct. Colb's point is that propensity data that might inform a bet before an accusation loses its value afterward (FRE 402).
Colb argues it is irrelevant, not merely prejudicial.
That's a different (state-of-mind) theory.
Wigmore's view is what shield laws rejected.
pre: Under Harriett Galvin's proposed rule, which bars a complainant's consensual sexual conduct with others only “to support the inference that a person who has previously engaged in consensual sexual conduct is for that reason more likely to consent,” which item excluded under the federal rule would most likely be admissible?

q: A student asks why a rape defendant's prior sexual assaults may be admitted under Rule 413 to prove propensity, while the complainant's prior consensual sex is barred under Rule 412. Which answer reflects the reasons given in class?
o: Shield laws encourage reporting, victims have privacy interests, and a victim's history cuts both ways.
Rule 412 is constitutionally required, while Rule 413 is only a policy choice by Congress.
A complainant's prior consent is more probative of consent than a defendant's prior assaults are of his guilt.
Rule 413 applies only in civil cases, where the risk of unfair prejudice is lower.
oe: Correct. These were the three distinctions on the Class 10 slides.
Neither rule is constitutionally required.
The reasoning runs the other way.
413 applies in criminal cases; 415 covers civil.

q: Before modern shield laws, which argument did courts and commentators use to justify cross-examining complainants about their sexual history?
o: That unchastity made consent likelier and a woman less credible; Wigmore urged examining every complainant.
That sexual history was relevant only to show the source of semen or other physical evidence.
That complainants had waived their privacy by reporting the alleged crime to the police.
That character evidence was otherwise inadmissible, so sexual history was the only credibility test.
oe: Correct. People v. Abbot and Wigmore reflect this view; State v. Sibley applied a double standard, holding a man's unchastity irrelevant to his veracity. Estrich described the resulting distrust of women.
That's a narrow modern exception, not the historical rationale.
Not the historical rationale discussed.
Courts treated sexual history as character evidence bearing on consent and credibility.
